en: Victory to the Blessed One, the Knower of the wombs of all living beings in the world, the Teacher of the world, the Delighter of the world, the Lord of the world, the Kinsman of the world; victory to the Grandfather of the world! — Nandī.1
Victory to the source of the scriptures, the last of the Tīrthaṅkaras;
victory, victory to the Guru of the worlds; victory to the Great Soul, Mahāvīra. (Nandī.2)
May there be well-being for the illuminator of the entire world; may there be well-being for the Jina Vīra;
may there be well-being for him who is honored by gods and asuras; may there be well-being for him whose passions are shaken off. — Nandī 3 —

May the auspicious city of the Saṅgha be blessed to you— filled with the jewels of scriptural knowledge, possessing the thoroughfare of pure right view, and having unbroken conduct as its ramparts. (Nandī 4)
Victory forever be to the Saṅgha-cakra, which has self-restraint and austerity as its hub, right belief as its rim, and is without rival— Nandī 5.

May there be prosperity for the Blessed One, the chariot of the Saṅgha, who has raised the banner of virtue, who is yoked with the horses of austerity and self-restraint, and whose sound is heard as he recites the sacred scriptures. —
Nandī 6.
[To him] who has emerged from the water of the mud of karma, whose long stalk is the jewel of learning,
whose firm pericarp is the five great vows, and whose filaments are the [spiritual] qualities. — Nandī 7.

May there be prosperity for the lotus of the Saṅgha, which is surrounded by the bees that are the lay disciples, which possesses the splendor of the sun-like Jina, and which has thousands of ascetics as its petals. — Nandī 8.

O Moon of the Saṅgha, whose mark is self-restraint and discipline, who is difficult to withstand for the Rāhu-like face of non-action— may you always be victorious, O you whose stainless light of right conviction is pure! — Nandī.9

May there be victory for the one who destroys the path of the heretics, whose appearance is radiant with the heat of austerity, who possesses the splendor of knowledge, and who is a hero among the community of the self-controlled. — Nandī 10

May there be prosperity for the Blessed One, the ocean of the Saṅgha, which is encompassed by the shore of steadfastness, whose course is the practice of recitation, which is unshakeable, and which is vast. (Nandī 11)
To him whose firm and deeply embedded pedestal is the excellent diamond of right vision, and who is adorned with the golden girdle of the jewel of the supreme Dharma. — Nandī 12.
Of the one whose jeweled peak shines and blazes like a polished golden stone slab,
and from whom the fragrant scent of virtue rises, enchanting like the Nandana grove. (Nandī.13)

To him who has drawn forth the lion-like leaders of sages from the beautiful caves of compassion for living beings, and whose mountain-caves are radiant with the jewels flowing from the ores of hundreds of logical arguments and with potent medicinal herbs. — Nandī 14.
[The temple] whose necklaces shine with waterfalls trickling from the excellent net of its vows, and whose mountain caves resound with the dancing peacocks that are the lay followers. (Nandī.

To the one whose mountain peak blazes with lightning-like flashes of the excellent method of the Vinaya, and who is a forest abounding in flowers and the fruit-bearing Kalpavṛkṣa trees of manifold virtues— Nandī 16.
I bow with humble prostration to the Great Mandara Mountain of the Saṅgha, which possesses a crest of pure beryl shining with the lovely light of the jewel of supreme knowledge;
its slopes are radiant with the jewels of virtue, fragrant with moral conduct, and adorned with austerity.
I pay homage to the Great Mandara Mountain of the Saṅgha, whose peak is the twelvefold Sūtra;
I pay homage to that treasury of the qualities of the Saṅgha, which is constantly compared to the city, the fourfold crossroads, the lotus, the moon, the sun, the ocean, and Mount Meru. (Nandī 17)
I pay homage to Ṛṣabha, Ajita, Sambhava, Abhinandana, Sumati, Suprabha, Supārśva, Candra, Puṣpadanta, Śītala, Śreyāṃsa, and Vāsupūjya. (Nandī. 18)
Vimala, Ananta, Dharma, Śānti, Kunthu, Ara, Malli, Munisuvrata, Nami, Nemi, Pārśva, and likewise Vardhamāna. — Nandī 19.
In this [assembly], Indrabhūti was first; then Agnibhūti was second; Vāyubhūti was third; and then Vyakta and Sudharman. (Nandī 20)
Maṇḍika, Māriyaputta, Akampita, Acalabhrātṛ,
Meyajja, and Prahlāda were the Gaṇadharas of Vīra. — Nandī 21.
Victorious forever is the teaching that is the path to liberation, which reveals all things as they truly are,
which destroys the intoxication of false doctrines, and which is the teaching of the supreme hero, the Lord of Jinas. — Nandī 22
I pay homage to Suhamma, Aggivessana, and Jambu named Kāsava; to Pabhava Kaccāyana and likewise to Vaccha born of Sijjambhava. (Nandī 23)
I pay homage to Yasobhadra of Tuṅgika, and to Sambhūta Māḍhara, Bhaddabāhu, Pāiṇṇa, Thūlabhadda, and Gōyama. — Nandī 24.
I pay homage to Mahāgiri of the Elāvaccasagotta clan, and then to Suhatthi; thereafter, I worship Bahula of the Kosiya clan, who is of equal age [to him]. (Nandī 25)
We pay homage to Hāriyagutta and Sāi; we pay homage to Hāriya and Sāmajja; and to Saṇḍilla of the Kosiya lineage, the venerable Jīyadhara. (Nandī 26)

I pay homage to the Venerable Samudra, whose fame has spread across the three oceans and who has mastered the vast expanse of all islands and seas; he is as unfathomably deep as the undisturbed ocean. (Nandī 27)

I pay homage to the venerable Āryamaṅgu, the speaker, the doer, the one who proclaims, and the one who brings forth the qualities of knowledge and vision; the steadfast one who has reached the further shore of the ocean of scripture. (Nandī 28)
I pay homage to Ajjadhamma; thereafter I pay homage to Bhaddagutta;
and thereafter to Ajjavaïra, who is equal to Vajra in the virtues of austerity and self-restraint. — Nandī 29
I pay homage to the venerable Arhat Rākṣita-kṣamaṇas, who protected their entire conduct; by them the *anuyoga* was guarded, which is like a casket for jewels. (Nandī. 30)
I bow my head in reverence to the venerable ascetic Nandila, whose mind is serene and who is constantly devoted to knowledge, vision, austerity, and discipline. — Nandī. 31
May the lineage of the Vācakas flourish— the illustrious lineage of the venerable Nāgahastin, who were preeminent in grammar, logic, the analysis of categories, and the *karmaprakṛti*. (Nandī 32)

May the lineage of the Vācakas named after the Revatī constellation flourish—those whose splendor is like that of collyrium and fresh clay, and who are the very source of the blue water-lilies of their pupils. (Nandī. 33)
Having departed from Ayodhyā, the wise lion of the Brahmadhvaja [monastery], a follower of the lineage of Kālikaśruta, attained the supreme rank of Vācaka. (Nandī 34)
I pay homage to those teachers, Khaṇḍila by name, whose tradition still prevails even today throughout half of Bharata, their fame having spread from many cities. (Nandī 35)
Therefore, we pay homage with our heads bowed to Himavanta, who possesses great valor, infinite courage and prowess, and who maintains infinite study of the scriptures. — Nandī 36
I pay homage to the teacher Nāgārjuna, the disciple of Kālika, the upholder of the *Suyagaḍāṅga-anuyoga* and the upholder of the *pūrvas*, and the ascetic of Himavat. (Nandī 37)

I pay homage to Nāgārjuna-vācaka, who was endowed with gentleness and humility, who attained the status of a teacher through gradual stages, and who was possessed of profound wisdom and scriptural conduct.

Homage also to the Govindas, who possess vast scriptural knowledge and supreme retention, who are ever endowed with forbearance and compassion, whose wisdom is difficult to surpass, who have bestowed the water of truth upon all beings, and who are never weary in their constant practice of austerity and self-restraint. — Nandī 38.

He is the color of pure gold and campaka flowers, like the interior of a choice lotus; he is the giver of joy to the hearts of living beings, an expert in the virtue of compassion, and steadfast. — Nandī 39.

The preeminent one in half-Bhārata, who has thoroughly mastered various types of sacred recitation (svādhyāya), the excellent bull among those well-versed in the scriptures, the bringer of joy to the lineage of the Nāila family— Nandī.40.
I pay homage again and again to the Ācārya Bhūyadinna, who brings about the destruction of the fear of worldly existence, and who was a disciple of the sage Nāgārjuna. (Nandī 41)

I pay homage to those who have well understood the eternal and the non-eternal, who maintain the meaning of the scriptures, and who manifest true reality therein— those who are being honored in the *Nandī*. 42.

I bow down with devotion to Dūṣagaṇi, who expounds the eight great goals, who brings about the liberation of the well-disciplined ascetics through his discourse, and whose voice is naturally sweet. — Nandī 43.
I bow to those feet of the Proclaimers, which have soles tender and delicate, praised for their auspicious marks, and saluted by hundreds of disciples. — Nandī 44
Having bowed my head to those other venerable ones who are devoted to the teachings of the son of Kālīya and are steadfast, I shall proclaim the exposition of knowledge. (Nandī 45)
A stone, a water-jar, a winnowing basket, a water-strainer, a swan, a buffalo, a ram, a mosquito, a leech, a cat, a mongoose, a cow, a drum, and a cowherd woman. (Nandī. 46)
Briefly, it is declared to be of three kinds, namely: that which is known, that which is unknown, and that which is ill-understood.
That which is known is as follows:
Just as swans extract milk from water, so too those who are enriched with heavy virtues here avoid faults; know that such an assembly is truly known. — Nandī 48.
As it was not understood, namely: // Nandī.49 //
That assembly which is naturally sweet, yet has become like a young deer, a lion,
or a cock, and remains unestablished like a jewel that is not recognized— such is the assembly.
(Nandī 50)
As for those who are ill-mannered:
// Nandī.51 // They are neither humble toward anyone, nor do they inquire [about others' welfare] due to the fault of pride.
Like a bladder filled with air, the village-wise man bursts [with pride].

(Nandī 52) Knowledge is declared to be fivefold; namely: sensory knowledge (*ābhinibodhika-jñāna*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta-jñāna*), clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhi-jñāna*), mind-reading knowledge (*manaḥparyāya-jñāna*), and omniscience (*kevala-jñāna*).
That [knowledge] is briefly declared to be of two kinds, namely: direct (pratyakṣa) and indirect (parokṣa).

What is direct perception (*paccakkha*)? Direct perception is declared to be of two kinds, namely: sensory direct perception (*indiyapaccakkha*) and non-sensory direct perception (*nōindiya-paccakkha*). What is sensory direct perception? Sensory direct perception is declared to be of five kinds, namely: auditory sensory direct perception, visual sensory direct perception, olfactory sensory direct perception, gustatory sensory direct perception, and tactile sensory direct perception. This is sensory direct perception.

What is that which is non-sensory direct perception (*nōindiyapaccakkha*)? Non-sensory direct perception is declared to be threefold; namely: sensory-clairvoyance direct perception (*ōhināṇapaccakkha*), mind-reading knowledge direct perception (*maṇapajjavanāṇapaccakkha*), and omniscience direct perception (*kēvalanāṇapaccakkha*).

What is direct perception through clairvoyance (*avadhijñāna*)? Direct perception through clairvoyance is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that which is innate to one's birth (*bhavapratyaya*) and that which arises from the subsidence and destruction of karma (*kṣayopaśamika*). What is that which is innate to one's birth? It belongs to two [classes of beings], namely: gods (*deva*) and denizens of hell (*nāraka*).

What is that which is produced by subsidence (*kṣayōpaśama*)? It belongs to two [categories]: humans and five-sensed animals. What is the cause for it being produced by subsidence? Through the destruction (*kṣaya*) of those obscuring karmas (*jñānāvaraṇīya-karma*) that have arisen, and through the subsidence (*upaśama*) of those that have not yet arisen, clairvoyance (*avadhijñāna*) arises.

Alternatively, avadhi-knowledge arises for a homeless ascetic (anagāra) who has attained the [necessary] qualities. Briefly, it is taught to be of six kinds, namely: following (ānugāmika), not following (anānugāmika), increasing (vaḍḍhamāṇaka), decreasing (hīyamāṇaka), regressive (paḍivāi), and non-regressive (appaḍivāi).
What is following avadhi-knowledge? Following avadhi-knowledge is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that which reaches the end (antagaya) and that which reaches the middle (majjhagaya).

What is that which is "gone to the end" (*antagaya*)? "Gone to the end" is declared to be threefold; namely: gone to the end in front, gone to the end behind, and gone to the end at the side. What is that which is "gone to the end in front"? "Gone to the end in front" is as follows: for example, a certain man might go along, repeatedly pushing forward a torch, a firebrand, a fire-brand, a jewel, a flame, or a lamp, keeping it in front of him. That is "gone to the end in front. What is that which is "gone to the end behind"? "Gone to the end behind" is as follows: for example, a certain man might go along, repeatedly pulling after him a torch, a firebrand, a fire-brand, a jewel, a flame, or a lamp, keeping it behind him. That is "gone to the end behind. What is that which is "gone to the end at the side"? "Gone to the end at the side" is as follows: for example, a certain man might go along, repeatedly drawing alongside a torch, a firebrand, a fire-brand, a jewel, a flame, or a lamp, keeping it at his side. That is "gone to the end at the side. That is "gone to the end."

What is that which is "situated in the middle" (*majjhagaya*)? "Situated in the middle" is as follows: suppose, for example, some man were to go about with a torch, a firebrand, a flame, a gem, a meteor, or a lamp held over his head. That is what is meant by "situated in the middle. Now, what is the distinction between "situated at the end" (*antagaya*) and "situated in the middle"? With clairvoyance situated at the front (*puraō antagaēṇaṁ*), one knows and sees only in front, across a distance of many hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, whether finite or infinite. With clairvoyance situated at the side (*pāsaō antagaēṇaṁ*), one knows and sees only to the side, across a distance of many hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, whether finite or infinite. With clairvoyance situated in the middle (*majjhagaēṇaṁ*), one knows and sees on all sides and in every direction, across a distance of many hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, whether finite or infinite. This is clairvoyance that is "concomitant" (*ānugāmiya*).
—End of Text—

What is non-attendant clairvoyance (*anānugāmiyaṃ ohi-nāṇaṃ*)? Non-attendant clairvoyance is as follows: suppose, for example, a certain man were to create one great mass of fire and, while moving around and around the very perimeter of that same mass of fire, sees that very mass of fire, but does not see it when he has gone elsewhere. In the same way, non-attendant clairvoyance knows and sees only at the place where it arises—whether it be a finite or infinite number of *yojanas*, whether connected or disconnected—but does not see it when one has gone elsewhere. That is non-attendant clairvoyance.

What is that increasing clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhi-jñāna*)? That clairvoyant knowledge increases in every direction and on all sides for one who abides in praiseworthy states of mental disposition, whose conduct is steady, and who is becoming purified, whose conduct is becoming purified.

The minimum extent of the avadhijñāna (clairvoyant knowledge) field is equal to the space occupied by a minute *panaka* living being that takes food for three moments; this is the minimum avadhikṣetra. (Nandī.

The supreme clairvoyance (paramōhī) regarding space is defined as follows: it is the extent of space in all directions that would be filled by the maximum number of fire-beings (aganijīvā) packed without any intervening gaps. (Nandī.
An *aṅgula* [is composed of] an incalculable fraction of an *āvalikā*; in two [cases], from an *āvalikā* up to an *aṅgula*, there are numerable [fractions];
[beyond that], an *āvalikā* [equals] a plurality of *aṅgulas*. — Nandī 67.
In the distance of a hand-span, a day is to be understood as a mere moment; at one *gavyūti*, it is a day;
at one *yojana*, it is many days; and at twenty-five [yojanas], it is a fortnight. — Nandī 68.
In Bharata, [the duration] is half a month; in Jambūdvīpa, it is declared to be one month;
in the world of humans, it is a year; and in Rucaka, it is many years. (Nandī 69)
In a calculable period of time, the islands and oceans are also calculable;
however, when the period of time is incalculable, the islands and oceans must be considered as indeterminate. (Nandī.
In the case of time, there is an increase of four; time must be considered in relation to the increase of space.
In the increase of space, substance and modes must be considered, as well as space and time.
(Nandī 71)
Time is subtle, and space is even more subtle than that;
within the measure of a single finger-breadth, there are infinite aeons of decrease (*osappiṇī*).
(Nandī 72)
Such is the increasing clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñāna*).

What is the decreasing clairvoyant knowledge? Decreasing clairvoyant knowledge is that which, for one who abides in unwholesome states of mental resolve, whose conduct is currently [unwholesome], and who is becoming defiled, whose conduct is becoming defiled—the range of clairvoyance (*avadhi*) diminishes from all sides and in every direction. Such is the decreasing clairvoyant knowledge.
— End of Text —

What is that which is limited (paḍivāi) clairvoyant knowledge (avadhijñāna)? Limited clairvoyant knowledge is that which, at its minimum, may perceive a fraction of an *aṅgula*—whether an innumerable part or a numerable part—or a hair-tip (*vālagga*), a plurality of hair-tips, a nit (*likkha*), a plurality of nits, a louse (*jūya*), a plurality of lice, a barley-corn (*java*), a plurality of barley-corns, a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), a plurality of finger-breadths, a foot (*pāya*), a plurality of feet, a span (*vihatthi*), a plurality of spans, a cubit (*rayaṇi*), a plurality of cubits, a forearm (*kucchi*), a plurality of forearms, a bow-length (*dhanu*), a plurality of bow-lengths, a quarter-mile (*gāuya*), a plurality of quarter-miles, a mile (*jōyaṇa*), a plurality of miles, a hundred miles, a plurality of hundreds of miles, a thousand miles, a plurality of thousands of miles, a hundred thousand miles, a plurality of hundreds of thousands of miles, ten million miles (*jōyaṇakōḍi*), a plurality of ten millions of miles, a billion miles (*jōyaṇakōḍākōḍi*), or a plurality of billions of miles; and at its maximum, it may perceive the entire world (*loga*). This is limited clairvoyant knowledge.

What is non-regressive clairvoyant knowledge (*apratipāti avadhi-jñāna*)? Non-regressive clairvoyant knowledge is that by which one knows and sees even a single point of space in the non-world (*aloka*); beyond that, it is non-regressive clairvoyant knowledge.
This is non-regressive clairvoyant knowledge.

That [clairvoyance] is taught to be fourfold in brief: by substance, by space, by time, and by state. Therein, by substance, a clairvoyant knows and sees, at the minimum, infinite material substances, and at the maximum, all material substances. By space, a clairvoyant knows and sees, at the minimum, an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and at the maximum, incalculable portions of the non-world (*aloka*) equal in size to the world (*loka*). By time, a clairvoyant knows and sees, at the minimum, an incalculable fraction of an *āvalikā*, and at the maximum, incalculable *osappiṇīs* (descending cycles) and *ussappiṇīs* (ascending cycles) of past and future time. By state, a clairvoyant knows and sees, at the minimum, infinite states, and at the maximum, also infinite states; he knows and sees an infinite fraction of all states.
Thus has been described the influx (*āsrava*) based on states of existence (*bhava-pratyaya*) and based on qualities (*guṇa-pratyaya*);
its many varieties [are further distinguished] according to substance (*dravya*), space (*kṣetra*), and time (*kāla*). — *Nandī*, 78.
Hell-beings, gods, and Tīrthaṅkaras possess vision that extends beyond their immediate surroundings; indeed, they see in every direction. The rest, however, see only in a limited area. (Nandī. 79)
Thus,
this is clairvoyant knowledge (avadhijñāna) as direct perception.

What is that? It is mind-reading knowledge (*manapajjavanāṇa*). Regarding mind-reading knowledge, O Venerable One, does it arise for humans or for non-humans? Goyama! For humans, not for non-humans. If for humans—does it arise for spontaneously born humans (*samucchima*) or for womb-born humans (*gabbhavakkantiya*)? Goyama! Not for spontaneously born humans, but for womb-born humans. If for womb-born humans—does it arise for womb-born humans of the karma-bhūmis, for womb-born humans of the non-karma-bhūmis, or for womb-born humans of the intermediate islands (*antaradīva*)? Goyama! For womb-born humans of the karma-bhūmis, not for womb-born humans of the non-karma-bhūmis, nor for womb-born humans of the intermediate islands. If for womb-born humans of the karma-bhūmis—does it arise for those with a lifespan of numerable years or for those with a lifespan of innumerable years? Goyama! For those with a lifespan of numerable years, not for those with a lifespan of innumerable years. If for those with a lifespan of numerable years of the karma-bhūmis who are womb-born—does it arise for those who are fully developed (*pajjattaga*) or for those who are not fully developed (*apajjattaga*)? Goyama! For those who are fully developed, not for those who are not fully developed.

If [it is asked] regarding fully developed human beings born from a womb in the karma-bhūmis with a lifespan of many years: are they those with right view, those with wrong view, or those with right-and-wrong view? Gautama! [It is] of fully developed human beings born from a womb in the karma-bhūmis with a lifespan of many years who possess right view; it is not of those with wrong view, nor of those with right-and-wrong view. If [it is asked] regarding fully developed human beings born from a womb in the karma-bhūmis with a lifespan of many years who possess right view: are they those with restrained right view, those with unrestrained right view, or those with partially restrained-right view? Gautama! [It is] of fully developed human beings born from a womb in the karma-bhūmis with a lifespan of many years who possess restrained right view; it is not of those with unrestrained right view, nor of those with partially restrained-right view.

If [it arises] for human beings who are restrained, with right view, fully developed, with a lifespan of many years, born from a womb, and belonging to the land of action (karmabhūmi), does it arise for those who are restrained but negligent, or for those who are restrained, with right view, fully developed, with a lifespan of many years, born from a womb, and belonging to the land of action? Gautama! It arises for human beings who are restrained, with right view, fully developed, with a lifespan of many years, born from a womb, and belonging to the land of action; it does not arise for human beings who are restrained but negligent. If [it arises] for human beings who are restrained, with right view, fully developed, with a lifespan of many years, born from a womb, and belonging to the land of action, does it arise for those who have attained psychic power (ṛddhiprāpta) and are restrained, with right view, fully developed, with a lifespan of many years, born from a womb, and belonging to the land of action, or for those who have not attained psychic power and are restrained, with right view, fully developed, with a lifespan of many years, born from a womb, and belonging to the land of action? Gautama! Mental direct knowledge (manahparyāyajñāna) arises for human beings who have attained psychic power, are restrained, with right view, fully developed, with a lifespan of many years, born from a womb, and belonging to the land of action; it does not arise for human beings who have not attained psychic power and are restrained, with right view, fully developed, with a lifespan of many years, born from a womb, and belonging to the land of action.

And that [knowledge] arises in two ways, namely: straight intellect (*ujjumaī*) and expanded intellect (*viulamaī*). In brief, it is declared to be fourfold: by way of substance (*davva*), by way of space (*khētta*), by way of time (*kāla*), and by way of state (*bhāva*). Therein, by way of substance, those with straight intellect know and see infinite aggregates consisting of infinite atoms; those with expanded intellect know and see those very same [aggregates], but to a greater degree, more extensively, more purely, and more clearly.

Regarding the field [of perception], Ujjumati knows and sees, at the minimum, an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum, downwards as far as the lowest stratum of this Jewel-Lustre Earth (*Rayaṇappabhā-puḍhavī*), upwards as far as the upper surface of the celestial realm (*jōisa*), and horizontally as far as the interior of the human realm (*antō-maṇussa-khētta*)—that is, within two and a half continents and oceans, in the fifteen lands of action (*kamma-bhūmi*), the thirty lands of non-action (*akamma-bhūmi*), and the fifty-six intermediate islands (*antaradīva*)—the mental states of conscious five-sensed beings who are fully developed. Vipulmati, however, knows and sees a field that is even more extensive, more vast, more pure, and more free from darkness than that of Ujjumati by two and a half *aṅgulas*.

As for Ujjumati, he knows and sees the past and future time, at the minimum for an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama* and at the maximum also for an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*. And Viulamaī knows and sees that very same [time] to an even greater extent, more extensively, more purely, and more free from darkness.

One of straightforward intellect knows and sees infinite states; he knows and sees an infinite fraction of all states. One of vast intellect, however, knows and sees those very same states to a greater degree, more extensively, more purely, and more free from darkness. Furthermore, mind-reading knowledge (manahparyāya-jñāna) is the manifestation of objects conceived by the minds of living beings.
Bound to the human realm and dependent upon virtues, it arises from the practice of conduct. (Nandī 83) —
This, then,
is mind-reading knowledge (*manahparyāyajñāna*).
— End of Section —

What is that? Perfect knowledge (*kevalajñāna*). Perfect knowledge is declared to be of two kinds, namely: perfect knowledge of those still in existence (*bhavastha-kevalajñāna*) and perfect knowledge of those who have attained liberation (*siddha-kevalajñāna*). What is that? Perfect knowledge of those still in existence. Perfect knowledge of those still in existence is declared to be of two kinds, namely: perfect knowledge of those still in existence with activity (*sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*) and perfect knowledge of those still in existence without activity (*ayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*). What is that? Perfect knowledge of those still in existence with activity. Perfect knowledge of those still in existence with activity is declared to be of two kinds, namely: perfect knowledge of those still in existence with activity at the first moment (*prathama-samaya-sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*) and perfect knowledge of those still in existence with activity at non-first moments (*aprathama-samaya-sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*); or alternatively, perfect knowledge of those still in existence with activity at the final moment (*carama-samaya-sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*) and perfect knowledge of those still in existence with activity at non-final moments (*acarama-samaya-sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*). This is that perfect knowledge of those still in existence with activity. What is that? Perfect knowledge of those still in existence without activity. Perfect knowledge of those still in existence without activity is declared to be of two kinds, namely: perfect knowledge of those still in existence without activity at the first moment (*prathama-samaya-ayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*) and perfect knowledge of those still in existence without activity at non-first moments (*aprathama-samaya-ayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*); or alternatively, perfect knowledge of those still in existence without activity at the final moment (*carama-samaya-ayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*) and perfect knowledge of those still in existence without activity at non-final moments (*acarama-samaya-ayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*). This is that perfect knowledge of those still in existence without activity.

What is that which is called perfected omniscience (*siddhakēvalanāṇa*)? Perfected omniscience is taught to be of two kinds, namely: the omniscience of those who have just attained perfection (*anantarasiddha-kēvalanāṇa*) and the omniscience of those who attained perfection in succession (*paramparasiddha-kēvalanāṇa*).

What is that? It is the knowledge of those who have attained perfection immediately thereafter (*anantara-siddha-kevalajñāna*). The knowledge of those who have attained perfection immediately thereafter is declared to be of fifteen kinds, namely: those perfected as founders of a *tīrtha* (*tīrtha-siddha*), those perfected not as founders of a *tīrtha* (*atīrtha-siddha*), those perfected as *tīrthaṃkaras* (*tīrthaṃkara-siddha*), those perfected not as *tīrthaṃkaras* (*atīrthaṃkara-siddha*), those perfected as self-enlightened ones (*svayaṃbuddha-siddha*), those perfected as individually enlightened ones (*pratyekabuddha-siddha*), those perfected through the enlightenment of a Buddha (*buddhabodhita-siddha*), those perfected with female gender (*strīliṅga-siddha*), those perfected with male gender (*puruṣaliṅga-siddha*), those perfected with neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga-siddha*), those perfected in their own [ascetic] garb (*saliṅga-siddha*), those perfected in another's garb (*anyaliṅga-siddha*), those perfected in the garb of a householder (*gṛhiliṅga-siddha*), those perfected alone (*eka-siddha*), and those perfected in groups (*aneka-siddha*). This is the knowledge of those who have attained perfection immediately thereafter.

What, then, is the omniscience of successively perfected beings (*paramparasiddhakēvalajñāna*)? The omniscience of successively perfected beings is declared to be of many kinds, namely: those perfected in the second moment, those perfected in the third moment, those perfected in the fourth moment, up to those perfected in the tenth moment, those perfected in a numerable number of moments, those perfected in an innumerable number of moments, and those perfected in an infinite number of moments. This is the omniscience of successively perfected beings; this is the omniscience of perfected beings.

Briefly, it is taught to be fourfold, namely: by substance, by space, by time, and by state. Therein, by substance, the one with omniscience (kevalajñānī) knows and sees all substances; by space, the one with omniscience knows and sees all space; by time, the one with omniscience knows and sees all time; and by state, the one with omniscience knows and sees all states.

Now, omniscient knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) is infinite, eternal, non-retrogressive, of one kind, and it is the cause for the communication of the states resulting from the transformation of all substances. (Nandī 90)

Having known the objects through kevalajñāna (omniscience), the Tīrthaṅkara speaks those things therein which are fit for exposition; that [speech] is his *vāgyoga-śruta* (scripture consisting of vocal activity); the remainder is not. — Nandī. 91
Such is that absolute knowledge; such is that direct perception.

What is indirect knowledge (*parokkha*)? Indirect knowledge is declared to be of two kinds, namely: indirect knowledge consisting of sensory-cognition (*ābhinibodhika-jñāna*) and indirect knowledge consisting of scriptural knowledge (*śruta-jñāna*). Where there is sensory-cognition, there is scriptural knowledge; where there is scriptural knowledge, there is sensory-cognition. Both of these are mutually concomitant; nevertheless, here the teachers explain a distinction: that which one perceives directly is sensory-cognition, while that which one hears is scriptural knowledge. Scriptural knowledge is preceded by the intellect (*mati*), but the intellect is not preceded by scriptural knowledge.

Non-specific mati consists of both mati-jñāna (cognitive knowledge) and mati-ajñāna (cognitive non-knowledge). Specific mati refers to the mati of one with right view, which is mati-jñāna, and the mati of one with wrong view, which is mati-ajñāna. Non-specific śruta consists of both śruta-jñāna (scriptural knowledge) and śruta-ajñāna (scriptural non-knowledge). Specific śruta refers to the śruta of one with right view, which is śruta-jñāna, and the śruta of one with wrong view, which is śruta-ajñāna.

What is that which is knowledge derived from mental perception (*ābhinibōhiya-nāṇa*)? Knowledge derived from mental perception is declared to be of two kinds, namely: that based on what has been heard (*suya-nissiya*) and that not based on what has been heard (*asuya-nissiya*). What is that which is not based on what has been heard? That which is not based on what has been heard is declared to be of four kinds, namely:
innate (*uppattiyā*), acquired through instruction (*vēṇaïyā*), produced by karma (*kammayā*), and transformative (*pāriṇāmiyā*).
Intellect is said to be fourfold; a fifth is not found.
(Nandī 96) [That intellect] which grasps an object that was previously unseen, unheard, and unexperienced, [attaining it] with purity at that very moment.
The intellect that possesses the fruit of being unshakeable is called "originary" (autpattikī). [Nandī 97] The examples are:
the Bharata stone, the merchant, the tree, the boy, the fall, the sarada bird, the body, and the excrement.
An elephant, a house, a ball, a pillar, a child, a woman on the road, a husband, and a son.
(Nandī 98) The Bharata stone, a ram, a cock, sesame seeds, sand, an elephant, a well, and a forest grove.
Milk-rice, a bowl, sweets, and five fathers. —
Nandī.99 Honey,
a lump of clay, a mark, a pot, alms-food, a servant, and a treasure.
Training in the treatises on the goal and desire for hundreds of thousands [of verses]— this is joy (Nandī 100).
[It is] capable of carrying one across the burden, having grasped the essence of the meaning of the three collections of scriptures.
The intellect arising from discipline bears fruit in both worlds.
(Nandī 101) In omens, the treatises on wealth, writing, arithmetic, and [the knowledge of] wells and horses...
The donkey, the mark, the knot, the goat, the chariot, and the courtesan.
Nandī.102 The white garment,
the long grass, and the lack of self-control belong to the crane.
The ox was roasted, and there was a fall from a tree by a horse.
(Nandī 103) Those who have seen the essence through right application [of knowledge], and whose minds are broadened by the thorough examination of the connection with karma...
Intelligence arises from karma as the fruit of success; it is found in the goldsmith, the ploughman, the potter, the fisherman, and the pearl-merchant and butter-seller. (Nandī 104)
The weaver, the potter, and the painter prosper when honored.
(Nandī 105) Inference is supported by reasons and examples; it concerns the consequences of speech and its transformation.
The intellect that bears the fruit of both the present benefit and the ultimate goal is called *pariṇāmikī*.
(Nandī 106) King Udiōdaya had a queen named Abhayā and a son named Siṭṭhi-kumāra.
The merchant Nandisena, the lay-disciple minister Dhanadatta, the forgiving son of a minister Cāṇakya, and Thūlabhadra. (Nandī 107)
In the cases of Nāsikka, Sundarī, and Nanda, the intellect undergoes transformation due to enmity.
In the cases of Calaṇāhaṇa, Āmaṇḍa, Maṇi, Sappa, Khaggī, and Thūbinda.
These and other such examples pertain to the transformative intellect (*pariṇāmikī-buddhi*).
This concludes that which is dependent on what has not been heard (*aśruta-niśrita*).
What is that which is based on scripture? It is declared to be fourfold, namely: apprehension (uggaha), speculation (īhā), judgment (avāya), and retention (dhāraṇā).

What is that? It is apprehension (*uggaha*). Apprehension is declared to be of two kinds, namely: apprehension of meaning (*atthuggaha*) and apprehension of the word-sound (*vañjaṇuggaha*). What is that? It is apprehension of the word-sound (*vañjaṇuggaha*). Apprehension of the word-sound is declared to be of four kinds, namely: apprehension of the word-sound by the sense of hearing, apprehension of the word-sound by the sense of smell, apprehension of the word-sound by the sense of taste, and apprehension of the word-sound by the sense of touch. This is apprehension of the word-sound.

What is the apprehension of meaning (*atthuggaha*)? The apprehension of meaning is declared to be sixfold, namely: apprehension of meaning by means of the sense-organ of hearing, apprehension of meaning by means of the sense-organ of sight, apprehension of meaning by means of the sense-organ of smell, apprehension of meaning by means of the sense-organ of taste, apprehension of meaning by means of the sense-organ of touch, and apprehension of meaning by means of the mind-organ (*no-indriya*).

For this [perception], there are these five synonymous designations with different sounds and different syllables, as follows: grasping (uggahaṇayā), retention (uvadhāraṇayā), hearing (savaṇayā), support (avalambaṇayā), and intelligence (mēhā).
This, then, is perception (uggaha).

What is that [which is] *īhā* (investigation)? *Īhā* is declared to be sixfold, namely: investigation by means of the sense of hearing, investigation by means of the sense of sight, investigation by means of the sense of smell, investigation by means of the sense of taste, investigation by means of the sense of touch, and investigation by means of the mind-sense (*no-indriya*). Regarding this, there are five synonymous designations with various sounds and various spellings, as follows: application (*ābhogaṇayā*), seeking (*maggaṇayā*), searching (*gavēsaṇayā*), reflection (*cintā*), and deliberation (*vīmaṁsā*). This is what constitutes *īhā*.

What is that? It is judgment (*avāya*). Judgment is declared to be sixfold, namely: judgment by means of the ear-faculty, judgment by means of the eye-faculty, judgment by means of the nose-faculty, judgment by means of the tongue-faculty, judgment by means of the body-faculty, and judgment by means of the mind-faculty. For this [judgment], there are these five synonymous names with different sounds and different syllables: turning toward (*āuṭṭaṇayā*), turning back (*paccāuṭṭaṇayā*), judgment (*avāya*), intellect (*buddhi*), and discernment (*viṇṇāṇa*).
This is what constitutes judgment.

What is retention (*dhāraṇā*)? Retention is declared to be sixfold, namely: retention of the ear-faculty, retention of the eye-faculty, retention of the nose-faculty, retention of the tongue-faculty, retention of the body-faculty, and retention of the mind-faculty. Regarding this, there are five synonymous designations with various sounds and various spellings, as follows: retention (*dhāraṇā*), commonality (*sādhāraṇā*), establishment (*ṭhavaṇā*), foundation (*païṭṭhā*), and storehouse (*kōṭṭhē*). This is retention.

Upon the acquisition of one *sāmāyika* [of perception], there is *īhā* (investigation) for the duration of one *muhūrta*, *avāya* (comprehension) for the duration of one *muhūrta*, and *dhāraṇā* (retention) for either a numerable or an innumerable period of time.

Thus, I shall provide an exposition of the twenty-eight-fold sensory cognition (*ābhinibodhika-jñāna*) regarding the apprehension of sounds (*vañjaṇa*), by means of the analogy of the awakening person and the analogy of the water jar. What is the analogy of the awakening person? Regarding the analogy of the awakening person: suppose a certain man were to awaken another sleeping man, saying, "So-and-so! So-and-so! Then, the questioner (*cōyaga*) says this to the teacher (*pannavaga*): "Do the soul-particles (*puggala*) that have entered [the sense organ] in one moment become apprehended? Or those that have entered in two moments... up to ten moments... or those that have entered in a numerable number of moments, or those that have entered in an innumerable number of moments? To the questioner who asks thus, the teacher replies: "No, those that have entered in one moment... no, those that have entered in two moments... up to no, those that have entered in a numerable number of moments; rather, it is the soul-particles that have entered in an innumerable number of moments that become apprehended. This is the analogy of the awakening person. What is the analogy of the water jar? Regarding the analogy of the water jar: suppose a certain man, taking a water jar from the mouth of a well, were to drop a single drop of water into it. That first drop vanishes; another is dropped, and that too vanishes. As more and more drops are being poured in, there will come a time when a drop of water remains in that jar; there will come a time when a drop of water fills that jar; there will come a time when a drop of water overflows that jar. In exactly the same way, as infinite soul-particles are being poured in, when that sound is filled, then he utters "Hum! Yet he does not yet know which specific sound it is. Then he enters into reflection (*īha*); then he knows, "This is so-and-so sound. Then he enters into comprehension (*avāya*); then it becomes fully understood (*uvagaya*). Then he enters into retention (*dhāraṇā*); then he retains it for a numerable or an innumerable period of time. Suppose, for example, a certain man hears an indistinct sound. That sound is apprehended as "sound," yet he does not yet know which specific sound it is. Then he enters into reflection; then he knows, "This is so-and-so sound. Then he enters into comprehension; then it becomes fully understood. Then he enters into retention; then he retains it for a numerable or an innumerable period of time.

Suppose, for example, that a certain man should see an indistinct form; he apprehends it as "a form. He should smell an indistinct odor; he apprehends it as "an odor. He should taste an indistinct flavor; he apprehends it as "a flavor. He should experience an indistinct touch; he apprehends it as "a touch," yet he does not yet know specifically what kind of touch this is. Then he enters into *īhā* (investigation), and then he knows, "This is such-and-such a touch. Then he enters into *avāya* (perception), and then it becomes fully understood (*uvagaya*). Then he enters into *dhāraṇā* (retention), and then he retains it for either a countable period of time or an incalculable period of time.

Suppose, for example, that a certain man experiences an indistinct dream; he apprehends it as "a dream," yet he does not yet know specifically what kind of dream it is. Then he enters into *īhā* (investigation), whereby he knows, "This is such-and-such a dream. Then he enters into *avāya* (perception), whereby it becomes fully understood (*uvagaya*). Then he enters into *dhāraṇā* (retention), whereby he retains it for either a countable period of time or an incalculable period of time. This is the illustration by means of the jar.

That [knowledge] is briefly declared to be fourfold, namely: by substance, by space, by time, and by state. Therein, by substance, the one possessing sensory-cognitive knowledge (ābhinibodhika-jñānin), through instruction, knows all substances but does not see them; by space, the one possessing sensory-cognitive knowledge, through instruction, knows all space but does not see it; by time, the one possessing sensory-cognitive knowledge, through instruction, knows all time but does not see it; by state, the one possessing sensory-cognitive knowledge, through instruction, knows all states but does not see them.
Apprehension, reflection, judgment, and retention— these are, in brief, the four constituent stages of sensory-cognitive knowledge (*ābhinibodhika-jñāna*). (Nandī 122)

In the Nandī, verse 123 states: "The grasping of an object is *avagraha*; the discernment of it here is *īhā*; the determination of it is *avāya*; and the retention of it, moreover, they call *dhāraṇā*."

Apprehension (*uggaha*) lasts for one moment; reflection (*īhā*) and judgment (*avāya*) last for half a muhūrta; and retention (*dhāraṇā*) should be known to last for an incalculable or a calculable period of time. (Nandī 124)
One hears a sound that has been contacted; one sees a form, however, which is not contacted.
But one should explain that odor, taste, and touch are experienced as being bound and contacted. — Nandī 125
The *samaseḍhī* [perception] hears sounds that are mixed with speech; however, the *viśeḍhī* [perception] hears sound only through the medium of *parāghāta* (impact). — Nandī 126.
Inquiry, exclusion, deliberation, searching, and investigation; perception, memory, intellect, and wisdom—all these constitute sensory-cognitive knowledge (*ābhinibodhika*). (Nandī 127)
Thus ends the knowledge derived from others through comprehension (ābhinibodhika-jñāna parokṣa).

What is that which is indirect knowledge through scripture (śrutajñāna-parokṣa)? Indirect knowledge through scripture is taught to be of fourteen kinds, namely: scriptural knowledge consisting of syllables (akṣara-śruta), scriptural knowledge not consisting of syllables (anakṣara-śruta), scriptural knowledge of sentient beings (saṃjñi-śruta), scriptural knowledge of non-sentient beings (asaṃjñi-śruta), right scriptural knowledge (samyaṅ-śruta), false scriptural knowledge (mithyā-śruta), scriptural knowledge with a beginning (sādi), scriptural knowledge without a beginning (anādi), scriptural knowledge with an end (saparyavasita), scriptural knowledge without an end (aparyavasita), scriptural knowledge that is finite (gamika), scriptural knowledge that is infinite (agamika), scriptural knowledge included within the limbs of the canon (aṅgapraviṣṭa), and scriptural knowledge not included within the limbs of the canon (anaṅgapraviṣṭa).

What is that which is scriptural knowledge consisting of syllables (*akkharasuya*)? Scriptural knowledge consisting of syllables is declared to be threefold; namely: the syllable as configuration (*saṇṇakkhara*), the syllable as phonetic expression (*vañjaṇakkhara*), and the syllable as attainment (*laddhiakkhara*). What is the syllable as configuration? The syllable as configuration is the shape and form of a syllable. This is the syllable as configuration. What is the syllable as phonetic expression? The syllable as phonetic expression is the vocal utterance of a syllable. This is the syllable as phonetic expression. What is the syllable as attainment? The syllable as attainment arises for one who has attained the capacity for syllables. It is as follows: the syllable as attainment of the ear-faculty, the syllable as attainment of the eye-faculty, the syllable as attainment of the nose-faculty, the syllable as attainment of the tongue-faculty, the syllable as attainment of the body-faculty, and the syllable as attainment of the mind-faculty (*noindriya*). This is the syllable as attainment. This is scriptural knowledge consisting of syllables. What is that which is scriptural knowledge not consisting of syllables (*anakkharasuya*)? Scriptural knowledge not consisting of syllables is declared to be of many kinds; namely: [as follows].
Exhalation, inhalation, belching, coughing, sneezing, and nasal discharge—
these, being without articulate syllables, are considered *chelīyāīya* (unintentional sounds). — Nandī 131.
Thus ends the Anakkharasuya (The Discourse on the Letterless).

What is that which is "with perception" (*saṇṇisuya*)? That which is with perception is declared to be threefold: namely, by way of instruction on time (*kāliovaēsa*), by way of instruction on cause (*heūvaēsa*), and by way of instruction on the doctrine of views (*diṭṭhivāovaēsa*). What is that by way of instruction on time? By way of instruction on time, one who possesses *īhā* (inquiry), *apōha* (elimination), *maggaṇā* (searching), *gavēsaṇā* (investigation), *cintā* (reflection), and *vīmaṁsā* (deliberation) is designated as "with perception"; one who does not possess *īhā*, *apōha*, *maggaṇā*, *gavēsaṇā*, *cintā*, and *vīmaṁsā* is designated as "without perception" (*asaṇṇī*). This is [the explanation] by way of instruction on time. What is that by way of instruction on cause? By way of instruction on cause, one who possesses the capacity for action preceded by intention (*abhisandhāraṇa*) is designated as "with perception"; one who does not possess the capacity for action preceded by intention is designated as "without perception. This is [the explanation] by way of instruction on cause. What is that by way of instruction on the doctrine of views? By way of instruction on the doctrine of views, through the subsidence-cum-destruction (*khaōvasama*) of the [obscuring] karma of that which is with perception, one is designated as "with perception. This is [the explanation] by way of instruction on the doctrine of views.
That is what is heard from those with consciousness; that is what is heard from those without consciousness.

What is right scripture (*sammasuya*)? Right scripture is that which has been proclaimed by the Arhats, the Blessed Ones, who possess arisen knowledge and vision, who are beholders, honored, and revered by the three worlds, who know the past, present, and future, and who are omniscient and all-seeing; it is the twelve-fold collection of the scriptures (*gaṇipiḍaga*), namely: the Āyāra, Sūyagaḍa, Ṭhāṇa, Samavāya, Vivāhapannattī, Nāyādhammakahā, Uvāsagadasā, Antagaḍadasā, Anuttarōvavāiyadasā, Paṇhāvāgaraṇa, Vivāgasuya, and Diṭṭhivāya. This twelve-fold collection of the scriptures is right scripture for one who possesses the fourteen *pūrvas* (*cōddasapuvvi*), and it is right scripture for one who possesses the ten *pūrvas* in their entirety (*abhinnadasapuvvi*). Beyond that, there is a distinction (*bhayaṇā*) among those who have broken [the *pūrvas*]. That, then, is right scripture.
—End of Text—

What, then, is false scripture (*micchasuya*)? False scripture is that which has been conceptualized by the ignorant who hold false views (*micchādiṭṭhi*), according to their own arbitrary intellect and imagination; namely: the *Bhārata*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Bhīmāsurutta*, the *Kauṭilya*, the *Sakaṭabhadrikā*, the *Ghoṭakamukha*, the *Kārpāsika*, the *Nāgasūkṣma*, the *Kanakasaptati*, the *Vaiśeṣika*, the *Buddhavacana*, the *Tairāśika*, the *Kāpila*, the *Lokāyata*, the *Sāṃkhya-tantra*, the *Māṭhara*, the *Purāṇa*, the *Vyākaraṇa*, the *Bhāgava*, the *Pāñjali*, the *Puṣyadevaka*, writing (*lēha*), arithmetic (*gaṇiya*), the cries of birds (*saüṇaruya*), drama (*nāḍaga*), and so forth; or else, the seventy-two arts (*bāvattarikalā*), the four Vedas with their ancillaries (*saṅgovaṅga*). These are false scripture for one of false view because they are embraced by falsehood (*micchatta*). For one of right view (*sammadiṭṭhi*), these very same works are right scripture (*sammasuya*) because they are embraced by rightness. Or rather, even for one of false view, these very same works are right scripture; why? Because they are a cause for rightness (*sammattahēuttaṇaō*); for when those of false view are urged by those very [right] principles, some abandon their own partisan views. That, then, is false scripture.
—End of Text—

What is that which has a beginning and an end, and that which is without beginning and without end? This twelve-fold collection of scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga gaṇipiṭaka*) is, from the perspective of the *vyuccheda-naya* (the standpoint of cessation), with a beginning and an end; from the perspective of the *avyuccheda-naya* (the standpoint of non-cessation), it is without beginning and without end. In brief, it is declared to be fourfold: by substance (*dravyataḥ*), by space (*kṣetrataḥ*), by time (*kālatāḥ*), and by state (*bhāvataḥ*). In that regard, by substance: with reference to a single individual, right hearing (*samyak-śruta*) has a beginning and an end; but with reference to many individuals, it is without beginning and without end. By space: with reference to the five regions of Bharata and the five regions of Airāvata, it has a beginning and an end; with reference to the five Great Videhas, it is without beginning and without end. By time: with reference to the *avasarpiṇī* and *utsarpiṇī* eras, it has a beginning and an end; with reference to the period that is neither *avasarpiṇī* nor *utsarpiṇī*, it is without beginning and without end. By state: when those states proclaimed by the Jinas are being described, explained, demonstrated, shown, illustrated, and pointed out at any given time, then with reference to those states, it has a beginning and an end. However, with reference to the state of subsided-destruction (*kṣayopaśamika*), it is without beginning and without end. Alternatively, the scripture of one destined for liberation (*bhavasiddhika*) has a beginning and an end, while the scripture of one not destined for liberation (*abhavasiddhika*) is without beginning and without end. The total number of syllables (*paryava-akṣara*) produced is infinite times the number of all spatial points of the entire universe. Furthermore, even for all living beings (*jīvas*), an infinite fraction of the syllable remains eternally uncovered. If even that were covered, the living being would become a non-living thing (*ajīvatva*). Even during the densest gathering of clouds, there is still light from the moon and the sun. This concludes that which has a beginning and an end; this concludes that which is without beginning and without end.

What is that which is based on tradition (*gamiya*)? What is that which is not based on tradition (*agamiya*)? That which is based on tradition is the *Diṭṭhivāda*; that which is not based on tradition is the *Kāliya-suya*. This is that which is based on tradition; this is that which is not based on tradition. Alternatively, it is briefly taught as being of two kinds, namely: that which is included within the *Aṅgas* (*aṅgapaviṭṭha*) and that which is outside the *Aṅgas* (*aṅgabāhira*).

What is that which is outside the scriptures (*aṅgabāhira*)? That which is outside the scriptures is declared to be twofold: namely, the essential duties (*āvassaya*) and that which is distinct from the essential duties (*āvassayavaïritta*). What is that which is the essential duties? The essential duties are declared to be sixfold: namely, the recitation of the fivefold formula (*sāmāiya*), the praise of the twenty-four [Tīrthaṅkaras] (*caüvīsatthaō*), the salutation (*vandaṇaya*), the confession (*paḍikkamaṇa*), the meditative posture (*kāussaggō*), and the renunciation (*paccakkhāṇa*). This is that which is the essential duties.

What is that which is outside the *āvaśyaka* (essential duties)? That which is outside the *āvaśyaka* is declared to be of two kinds, namely: *kālika* (to be studied at specific times) and *utkālika* (to be studied at all times). What is that which is *utkālika*? The *utkālika* is declared to be of many kinds, namely: the *Daśavaikālika*, the *Kappiyākappiya*, the *Cullakappasuya*, the *Mahākappasuya*, the *Ovāiya*, the *Rāyapasēṇiya*, the *Jīvābhigama*, the *Pannavaṇā*, the *Mahāpannavaṇā*, the *Pamāyappamāya*, the *Nandī*, the *Anuōgadārāiṁ*, the *Dēvindatthaō*, the *Tandulavēyāliya*, the *Candāvējjhaya*, the *Sūrapannattī*, the *Pōrisimaṇḍala*, the *Maṇḍalapavēsa*, the *Vijjācaraṇaviṇicchaō*, the *Gaṇivijjā*, the *Jhāṇavibhattī*, the *Maraṇavibhattī*, the *Āyavisōhī*, the *Maraṇavisōhī*, the *Vīyarāgasuya*, the *Saṁlēhaṇāsuya*, the *Vihārakappa*, the *Caraṇavihī*, the *Āurapaccakkhāṇa*, the *Mahāpaccakkhāṇa*, and so forth. This is what is called the *utkālika*.

What is that which is called *kāliya*? *Kāliya* is declared to be of many kinds, namely: the *Uttarajjhayaṇas*, the *Dasās*, the *Kappa*, the *Vavahāra*, the *Nisīha*, the *Mahānisīha*, the *Isibhāsiyāiṃ*, the *Jambuddīvapannattī*, the *Dīvasāgarapannattī*, the *Candapannattī*, the *Khuḍḍiyāvimāṇapavibhattī*, the *Mahalliyāvimāṇapavibhattī*, the *Aṅgacūliyā*, the *Vaggacūliyā*, the *Vivāhacūliyā*, the *Aruṇōvavāē*, the *Varuṇōvavāē*, the *Garulōvavāē*, the *Dharaṇōvavāē*, the *Vēsamaṇōvavāē*, the *Velandharōvavāē*, the *Dēvindōvavāē*, the *Uṭṭhāṇasuē*, the *Samuṭṭhāṇasuē*, the *Nāgapariyāvaṇiyāō*, the *Nirayāvaliyāō*, the *Kappiyāō*, the *Kappavaḍaṁsiyāō*, the *Pupphiyāō*, the *Pupphacūliyāō*, and the *Vaṇhidasāō*.

There are eighty-four thousand *païnnas* (proclamations) of the Blessed Arhat Usabhasāmī, the first Tīrthaṅkara; likewise, there are countless thousands of *païnnas* for the intermediate Jinas; and there are fourteen thousand *païnnas* of the Blessed Vardhamānasāmī. Alternatively, whatever number of disciples possessed the fourfold intelligence—namely, the innate (*uppattiyā*), the acquired (*vēṇaïyā*), the karmic (*kammayā*), and the transformative (*pāriṇāmiyā*)—there were that many thousands of *païnnas* for him. The Pratyekabuddhas were also exactly that many. Such is the Kālika [scripture]; such is that which is outside the Āvaśyaka; such is the Anaṅgapraviṣṭa [literature].

What is that which is included in the *Aṅgas*? The *Aṅga*-included scriptures are declared to be twelvefold, namely: the *Ācārāṅga*, the *Sūtrakṛtāṅga*, the *Sthānāṅga*, the *Samavāyāṅga*, the *Vyākhyāprajñapti*, the *Jñātṛdharmakathā*, the *Upāsakadaśā*, the *Antakṛddaśā*, the *Anuttaraupapātikadaśā*, the *Praśnavyākaraṇa*, the *Vipākaśruta*, and the *Dṛṣṭivāda*.

What is that [treatise] called Āyāra (Conduct)? In Āyāra, the conduct, range of activity, discipline, modesty, training, speech, non-speech, behavior, actions, origins, modes of livelihood, and so forth of the Śramaṇas and Nirgranthas are declared. It is briefly explained as being fivefold, namely: the conduct of knowledge (jñānācāra), the conduct of vision (darśanācāra), the conduct of character (cāritrācāra), the conduct of austerity (tapācāra), and the conduct of energy (vīryācāra). In Āyāra, there are limited recitations (vācanās), numerable sub-sections (anuyogadvāras), numerable sections (veḍhas), numerable verses (ślokas), numerable summaries (niryuktis), and numerable detailed expositions (pratipattis). As for its status as an Aṅga, it is the first Aṅga; it consists of two books (śrutaskandhas), twenty-five chapters (adhyāyas), eighty-five times for recitation (uddeśanakālas), eighty-five times for re-recitation (samuddeśanakālas), and eighteen thousand words by count of words. There are numerable syllables, infinite scriptures (āgamas), infinite aspects (paryāyas), limited mobile beings (trasas), and infinite stationary beings (sthāvaras). The eternal, pre-established, bound, and accumulated entities proclaimed by the Jinas are declared, explained, demonstrated, shown, and pointed out therein. Thus is the Self (Ātman); thus is it known; thus is it understood; thus is the exposition of conduct and action declared. This, then, is Āyāra.

The Bodhisattva’s Skillful Means in Gathering Disciples Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, he does so by means of skillful methods. He does not teach the Dharma by means of pride, nor by means of arrogance, nor by means of hypocrisy, nor by means of flattery, nor by means of seeking gain, honor, or fame. Rather, he teaches the Dharma solely out of compassion for sentient beings, with a mind free from attachment, and with the intention of establishing them in the Buddha-dharma. In this regard, Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while teaching the Dharma, should harbor thoughts of self-importance or look down upon others, he does not possess skillful means. If he seeks only his own benefit and neglects the welfare of others, he does not possess skillful means. If he teaches the profound Dharma to some while teaching only the superficial Dharma to others based on their dispositions, yet does so with a mind of partiality rather than impartiality, he does not possess skillful means. However, Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having first established all sentient beings in the roots of virtue, subsequently teaches them the Dharma according to their individual capacities—whether they require the vehicle of the Hearers, the Pratyekabuddhas, or the Mahāyāna—and does so with a mind of great compassion that views all beings as equal, then he possesses skillful means. Moreover, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses skillful means does not abandon sentient beings even if they commit the five heinous crimes or hold wrong views. He approaches them with the thought, "I shall lead these beings to maturity through various skillful methods," and thus he never turns away from his vow to liberate them. This, Mañjuśrī, is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful means in gathering disciples.

What is that *Sūyagaḍa*? In the *Sūyagaḍa*, the world (*loka*) is explained, the non-world (*aloka*) is explained, the world-and-non-world (*lokāloka*) is explained; living beings (*jīva*) are explained, non-living beings (*ajīva*) are explained, living-and-non-living beings (*jīvājīva*) are explained; one's own doctrine (*sasamaya*) is explained, the doctrines of others (*parasamaya*) are explained, and both one's own and others' doctrines are explained. In the *Sūyagaḍa*, having refuted one hundred systems of those who maintain the existence of action (*kiriyāvāī*), eighty-four of those who deny action (*akiriyāvāī*), sixty-seven of those who hold to ignorance (*annāṇiyavāī*), thirty-two of those who follow the Vedic tradition (*vēṇaïyavāī*), and three hundred and sixty-three of those who hold evil views (*pāvāduya*), it establishes one's own doctrine. The *Sūyagaḍa* has a limited number of recitations (*vāyaṇā*), a numerable number of analytical expositions (*anuōgāra*), a numerable number of sections (*vēḍha*), a numerable number of verses (*silōga*), a numerable number of summaries (*nijjuttī*), and a numerable number of detailed discussions (*paḍivattī*). In terms of its structural status as an *aṅga*, it is the second *aṅga*. It consists of two *suyakkhandhas*, twenty-three chapters (*ajjhayaṇa*), thirty-three times for introductory recitation (*uddēsaṇakāla*), thirty-three times for concluding recitation (*samuddēsaṇakāla*), and thirty-six thousand phrases (*paya*) by count of words. It contains a numerable number of syllables, infinite modes (*gamā*), and infinite aspects (*pajjava*). Therein, finite mobile beings (*tasā*) and infinite stationary beings (*thāvarā*)—eternal, pre-existing, bound, and accumulated states proclaimed by the Jinas—are described, explained, demonstrated, shown, pointed out, and illustrated. Thus is the self (*āyā*); thus is it known; thus is it understood; thus is the exposition of conduct (*caraṇa*) and discipline (*karaṇa*) described. This is the *Sūyagaḍa*.
—End of Text—

What is that [which is called] *Ṭhāṇa*? In *Ṭhāṇa*, living beings (*jīva*) are established; non-living beings (*ajīva*) are established; both living and non-living beings are established. One's own doctrine (*sasamaya*) is established; another's doctrine (*parasamaya*) is established; both one's own and another's doctrines are established. The world (*loka*) is established; the non-world (*aloka*) is established; both the world and the non-world are established. In *Ṭhāṇa*, cliffs, peaks, mountains, ridges, summits, valleys, caves, mines, lakes, and rivers are described. In *Ṭhāṇa*, the exposition of categories (*bhāva*) increased by ten through a sequence of single units starting from one is described. In *Ṭhāṇa*, there are a limited number of recitations (*vāyaṇā*), a numerable number of sections on subordinate gates (*anuogadāra*), a numerable number of chapters (*veḍha*), a numerable number of verses (*silōga*), a numerable number of analytical expositions (*nijjuttī*), a numerable number of summaries (*saṅgahaṇī*), and a numerable number of sub-sections (*paḍivattī*). In terms of its status as an *Aṅga*, it is the third *Aṅga*. It consists of one book (*suyakkhandha*), ten chapters (*ajjhayaṇa*), twenty-one periods for recitation (*uddesaṇakāla*), twenty-one periods for re-recitation (*samuddesaṇakāla*), seventy-two thousand phrases (*payasahassa*) by count of words, a numerable number of syllables (*akkhara*), infinite modes (*gamā*), and infinite aspects (*pajjava*). Therein, limited mobile beings (*tasā*) and infinite stationary beings (*thāvarā*)—eternal, pre-existing, bound, and accumulated states proclaimed by the Jinas—are described, explained, expounded, shown, demonstrated, and illustrated. Thus is the self (*āyā*), thus is it known, thus is it understood, and thus is the exposition of conduct and practice (*caraṇa-karaṇa*) described. This is *Ṭhāṇa*.
— End of Document —

What is the *Samavāya*? In the *Samavāya*, living beings (*jīva*) are enumerated; non-living beings (*ajīva*) are enumerated; both living and non-living beings are enumerated; one's own doctrine (*sasamaya*) is enumerated; another’s doctrine (*parasamaya*) is enumerated; both one’s own and another’s doctrines are enumerated; the world (*loka*) is enumerated; the non-world (*aloka*) is enumerated; both the world and the non-world are enumerated. In the *Samavāya*, the exposition of categories (*bhāva*) beginning with one and increasing by one up to a hundred places is declared. Furthermore, it is enumerated as the "sprout-path" (*pallavamagga*) of the twelvefold collection of scriptures (*gaṇipiḍaga*). The *Samavāya* has a limited number of recitations (*vāyaṇā*), a numerable number of sections on subordinate gates (*anuogadāra*), a numerable number of chapters (*veḍha*), a numerable number of verses (*silōga*), a numerable number of analytical expositions (*nijjuttī*), a numerable number of summaries (*saṅgahaṇī*), and a numerable number of refutations (*paḍivattī*). In terms of the Angas, it is the fourth Anga. It consists of one scriptural section (*suyakkhandha*), one lesson (*ajjhayaṇa*), one time for recitation (*uddēsaṇakāla*), and one time for detailed recitation (*samuddēsaṇakāla*). It contains forty-four hundred thousand phrases (*payasayasahassa*) in terms of phrasing (*payagga*), a numerable number of syllables (*akkhara*), infinite modes (*gamā*), and infinite aspects (*pajjava*). Therein, finite mobile beings (*tasā*) and infinite stationary beings (*thāvarā*) are enumerated; eternal, fixed, bound, and accumulated states (*bhāvā*) proclaimed by the Jinas are declared, and so forth, up to being demonstrated. Thus is the self (*āyā*), thus is it known (*nāyā*), thus is it understood (*viṇṇāyā*). Thus is the exposition of conduct and practice (*caraṇa-karaṇa-parūvaṇā*) declared. This is the *Samavāya*.
— End of Text —

What, then, is the *Vyākhyāprajñapti*? In the *Vyākhyāprajñapti*, living beings (*jīva*) are explained, non-living beings (*ajīva*) are explained, both living and non-living beings are explained; its own doctrine (*sasamaya*) is explained, the doctrines of others (*parasamaya*) are explained, both its own and others' doctrines are explained; the world (*loka*) is explained, the non-world (*aloka*) is explained, and the world-and-non-world are explained. The *Vyākhyāprajñapti* has a limited number of recitations (*vācanā*), a numerable number of sections on subordinate subjects (*anuyogadvāra*), a numerable number of chapters (*veḍha*), a numerable number of verses (*śloka*), a numerable number of analytical expositions (*niryukti*), a numerable number of summaries (*saṅgrahaṇī*), and a numerable number of discourses (*pratipatti*). In terms of its constituent parts (*aṅga-arthatā*), it is the fifth *aṅga*. It consists of one book (*suyakkhandha*), slightly more than one hundred chapters (*adhyayana*), ten thousand sections (*uddeśaka*), ten thousand sub-sections (*samuddeśaka*), thirty-six thousand explanations (*vyākaraṇa*), two hundred and eighty-eight thousand words (*pada*) by measure of words. It contains a numerable number of syllables (*akṣara*), infinite modes (*gama*), infinite aspects (*paryāya*), a limited number of mobile beings (*trasa*), and infinite immobile beings (*sthāvara*). Eternal, pre-existing, fixed, and organized states as proclaimed by the Jinas are therein described, explained, demonstrated, shown, pointed out, and illustrated. Thus is the Self (*ātman*), thus is knowledge (*jñāna*), thus is realization (*vijñāna*), and thus is the exposition of conduct and practice (*caraṇa-karaṇa-prarūpaṇā*) described. This, then, is the *Vyākhyāprajñapti*.

—The Great Vehicle Sutra of the Ten Wheels of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva— At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas: "Good sons, there is a dharma-gate called 'The Ten Wheels of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. If there are sentient beings who hear this dharma-gate, they shall all attain liberation. What are these ten wheels? First is the wheel of the roots of goodness; second is the wheel of the pure precepts; third is the wheel of patience and forbearance; fourth is the wheel of diligence and vigor; fifth is the wheel of meditative concentration; sixth is the wheel of wisdom; seventh is the wheel of skillful means; eighth is the wheel of vows; ninth is the wheel of power; and tenth is the wheel of knowledge. If there are sentient beings who, having heard this dharma-gate, can practice even a single wheel among these ten, they shall not fall into the three evil realms for one hundred thousand kalpas. If they can practice two wheels, they shall not fall into the three evil realms for two hundred thousand kalpas. If they can practice three wheels, they shall not fall into the three evil realms for three hundred thousand kalpas. If they can practice four wheels, they shall not fall into the three evil realms for four hundred thousand kalpas. If they can practice five wheels, they shall not fall into the three evil realms for five hundred thousand kalpas. If they can practice six wheels, they shall not fall into the three evil realms for six hundred thousand kalpas. If they can practice seven wheels, they shall not fall into the three evil realms for seven hundred thousand kalpas. If they can practice eight wheels, they shall not fall into the three evil realms for eight hundred thousand kalpas. If they can practice nine wheels, they shall not fall into the three evil realms for nine hundred thousand kalpas. If they can practice all ten wheels, they shall never again fall into the three evil realms throughout the course of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. Furthermore, good sons, if there are sentient beings who, having heard this dharma-gate, can uphold it, read it, recite it, explain it to others, or practice it according to the teaching, they shall, at the end of their lives, see Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva appear before them. He will take them by the hand and lead them to rebirth in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions, where they shall dwell in peace and happiness. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "The roots of goodness are the first wheel, Pure precepts are the second wheel, Patience and forbearance are the third wheel, Diligence and vigor are the fourth wheel, Meditative concentration is the fifth wheel, Wisdom is the sixth wheel, Skillful means are the seventh wheel, Vows are the eighth wheel, Power is the ninth wheel, And knowledge is the tenth wheel. If one practices even one of these ten wheels, One shall not fall into the three evil realms for a hundred thousand kalpas. If one practices two, three, four, or five, Or six, seven, eight, nine, or ten, The retribution for evil deeds shall gradually diminish, Until finally one attains liberation. If one hears, upholds, reads, or recites, And explains it to others according to the teaching, At the end of life, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Will appear before them and lead them away. He will take them to the presence of the Buddhas, Where they shall dwell in peace and happiness. When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the assembly of great bodhisattvas, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. —The Great Vehicle Sutra of the Ten Wheels of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva—End.

What, then, are the *Nāyādhammakahāo* (Discourses on the Teachings of the Jinas)? In the *Nāyādhammakahāo*, there are narrated the cities of the Jinas, their gardens, shrines, groves, and assembly halls; their kings, mothers, fathers, and spiritual teachers; their religious discourses; their worldly and otherworldly specific attainments (*ṛddhi-viśeṣa*); their renunciations of enjoyments, their initiations, their stages of wandering, their mastery of the scriptures, their ascetic practices, their purifications (*saṃlekhanā*), their renunciations of food, their fasts unto death, their journeys to the celestial realms, their rebirths in noble families, their subsequent attainment of enlightenment, and their final liberation. There are ten sections (*varga*) of these religious discourses. In each discourse, there are five hundred narratives (*ākhyāyikā-śata*); in each narrative, five hundred sub-narratives (*upākhyāyikā-śata*); and in each sub-narrative, five hundred further sub-sub-narratives (*ākhyāyikopākhyāyikā-śata*). Thus, including the preceding and following parts, it is declared that there are eighty-four million narrative units (*kathā-aṅga-koṭi*). The *Nāyādhammakahāo* have a finite number of recitations (*vācanā*), a finite number of analytical gates (*anuyoga-dvāra*), a finite number of chapters (*veḍha*), a finite number of verses (*śloka*), a finite number of summaries (*niryukti*), a finite number of compendiums (*saṅgrahaṇī*), and a finite number of perspectives (*pratipatti*). In terms of its status as an *aṅga*, it is the sixth *aṅga*. It consists of two scriptural divisions (*śrutaskandha*), nineteen chapters (*adhyayana*), nineteen periods for instruction (*uddeśanakāla*), and nineteen periods for review (*samuddeśanakāla*). It contains a finite number of thousands of phrases (*pada-sahasra*) by measure of words, and a finite number of syllables. The states proclaimed by the Jina are narrated therein. Thus is the self proclaimed; thus is it narrated. These are the *Nāyādhammakahāo*.
— End of Text —

What, then, are the *Upāsakadaśās*? In the *Upāsakadaśās*, there are proclaimed: the cities of the lay-disciples (*śramaṇopāsaka*), their gardens, shrines (*caitya*), groves, assemblies (*samavasaraṇa*), kings, parents, teachers of the Dharma, religious discourses (*dharmakathā*), distinctions of worldly and otherworldly prosperity, renunciations of enjoyments, stages of the religious life (*paryāya*), mastery of the scriptures, practices of austerity, the undertaking of vows, restraints, virtues, prohibitions, renunciations, fasts and observances (*poṣadhopavāsa*), the various vows (*pratimā*), afflictions (*upasarga*), processes of self-mortification (*saṃlekhanā*), renunciations of food, voluntary entry into the final state (*pādopagamana*), departures to the celestial realms, rebirths in noble families, further attainment of enlightenment (*bodhilābha*), and final liberation (*antakriyā*). The *Upāsakadaśās* have a limited number of recitations (*vācanā*), a numerable number of sections (*anuyogadvāra*), a numerable number of chapters (*veḍha*), a numerable number of verses (*śloka*), a numerable number of analytical summaries (*niryukti*), a numerable number of compendiums (*saṅgrahaṇī*), and a numerable number of sub-divisions (*pratipatti*). As for its status as an *Aṅga*, it is the seventh *Aṅga*; it consists of one book (*śrutaskandha*), ten chapters (*adhyayana*), ten periods of exposition (*uddeśanakāla*), and ten periods of counter-exposition (*samuddeśanakāla*). It contains a numerable number of thousands of words by word-count, a numerable number of syllables, infinite modes (*gama*), and infinite aspects (*paryāya*). Therein are proclaimed the finite mobile beings and the infinite stationary beings—the eternal, fixed, bound, and accumulated states as taught by the Jinas. Thus is the Self known; thus is it understood; thus is it fully comprehended; thus is the exposition of conduct and practice (*caraṇa-karaṇa*) proclaimed. These, then, are the *Upāsakadaśās*.

The Bodhisattva’s Ten Grounds (Daśabhūmika) Chapter One: The Ground of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the great city of Rājagṛha, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of five thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—free from outflows, free from afflictions, fully liberated in mind, and fully liberated through wisdom; who had accomplished their task, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose minds were liberated through perfect knowledge, like great nāgas, with the divine eye, with the divine ear, knowing the minds of others, possessing the power of recollection of past lives, and having attained mastery over the supernormal powers. There were also many thousands of bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, all of whom were irreversible, possessed of the marks of irreversibility, and endowed with the dhāraṇīs and samādhis. At that time, the Blessed One, surrounded by this great assembly and honored by them, sat upon his lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having attained supreme, perfect enlightenment. He was emitting a vast, immeasurable light from his body, illuminating the entire world-system, surpassing the splendor of the sun, moon, and all the gods. Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and said to him: “Blessed One, it is wonderful how the Tathāgata, having attained supreme, perfect enlightenment, emits such a vast light, illuminating the entire world-system. The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, it is because the Tathāgata wishes to reveal the profound and vast Dharma, which is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, for the sake of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas. Ānanda, there are ten grounds of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are: the Ground of Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Refulgence, the Ground of Blazing, the Ground of Difficult to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Intelligence, and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma. These, Ānanda, are the ten grounds of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas.
