[The Buddha then proceeded to explain each of these grounds in detail, describing the qualities, practices, and realizations of the bodhisattvas dwelling upon them. [End of Chapter One] Chapter Two: The Ground of Purity (Vimalā-bhūmi) [The Buddha continued: “Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the second ground, he becomes purified in ten ways. What are these ten? They are: purification of intention, purification of thought, purification of conduct, purification of view, purification of discipline, purification of resolve, purification of effort, purification of diligence, purification of skillful means, and purification of wisdom. Having attained these purifications, the bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes established in the second ground, the Ground of Purity. [The Buddha then described the specific perfections, meditative concentrations, and insights cultivated by the bodhisattva on this ground. [End of Chapter Two] ... [and so on through the remaining nine grounds] ... Chapter Ten: The Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi) [The Buddha concluded: “Ānanda, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the tenth ground, the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, he has perfected all the qualities of the bodhisattvas and is on the verge of attaining the state of a Tathāgata. He possesses the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion. Having fulfilled all the accumulations of merit and wisdom, he is able to turn the wheel of the Dharma, liberating countless beings from suffering. This, Ānanda, is the tenth ground of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One entered into a state of meditative concentration called "The Light of the Dharma," and from his body issued forth a great radiance that filled the entire universe. All the worlds were transformed into a single field of jewels, and the sounds of the Dharma resounded everywhere. Then the venerable Ānanda, having heard this teaching on the ten grounds of the bodhisattvas, was filled with joy and faith. He bowed down at the feet of the Blessed One and departed. The entire assembly, having heard the Blessed One’s exposition, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. Thus ends the Daśabhūmika Sūtra.

What, then, are the *Antagaḍadasāo*? In the *Antagaḍadasāo*, there are described the cities, gardens, shrines, groves, assemblies, kings, parents, teachers of the Dharma, religious discourses, specific worldly and otherworldly powers, renunciations of enjoyments, initiations, stages of the wandering life, mastery of the scriptures, practices of austerity, processes of self-examination (*saṃlekhanā*), renunciations of food, voluntary entry into the final fast, and the final liberation (*antakriyā*). The *Antagaḍadasāo* have a limited number of recitations (*vācanā*), a numerable number of sub-sections (*anuyogadvāra*), a numerable number of sections (*veḍha*), a numerable number of verses (*śloka*), a numerable number of analytical expositions (*niryukti*), a numerable number of summaries (*saṅgrahaṇī*), and a numerable number of chapters (*pratipatti*). As for its status as an *Aṅga*, it is the eighth *Aṅga*; it consists of one book (*suyakkhandha*), eight chapters (*varga*), eight times for recitation (*uddesaṇakāla*), and eight times for detailed recitation (*samuddesaṇakāla*). It contains thousands of words by count of words, numerable syllables, infinite modes (*gama*), infinite aspects (*paryāya*), a limited number of mobile beings (*trasa*), and infinite stationary beings (*sthāvara*). The eternal, pre-established, bound, and accumulated states proclaimed by the Jinas are described, explained, and so forth, up to being demonstrated. These are the *Anuttarovavāiyadasā*.

How much more so if they were to study it, recite it, and practice it accordingly. This is because the perfection of wisdom is the mother, the progenitor, and the nurse of the Bodhisattvas, and it is by means of this that they attain the state of omniscience. Subhūti, suppose a man were to take a measure of sesame seeds from a great mountain of sesame seeds one yojana high and one yojana wide. If he were to remove a single seed every hundred years, Subhūti, do you think that the lifespan of that man would be long? Subhūti replied, "Indeed, Blessed One, it would be very long. The Blessed One said, "Even longer than that, Subhūti, is the lifespan of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. What, then, are the *Paṇhāvāgaraṇāiṃ* (Questions and Explanations)? In the *Paṇhāvāgaraṇāiṃ*, there are one hundred and eight questions, one hundred and eight non-questions, and one hundred and eight questions-and-non-questions; there are questions concerning the thumb, questions concerning the arm, and questions concerning the mirror; and various other divine wonders and supernatural powers (*vijjāisaya*) are proclaimed in divine dialogues with Nāgas and Suvannas. Of the *Paṇhāvāgaraṇāiṃ*, there are limited recitations (*vāyaṇā*), numerable sub-sections (*anuōgadāra*), numerable *vēḍhas*, numerable verses (*silōga*), numerable *nijjuttis*, numerable summaries (*saṅgahaṇī*), and numerable chapters (*paḍivattī*). As for its status as an *aṅga*, it is the tenth *aṅga*; it consists of one *suyakkhandha*, forty-five chapters (*ajjhayaṇa*), forty-five times for recitation (*uddēsaṇakāla*), and forty-five times for review (*samuddēsaṇakāla*); it contains numerable thousands of words by word-count, numerable syllables, infinite modes (*gamā*), and infinite aspects (*pajjavā*); it proclaims numerable mobile beings (*tasā*) and infinite stationary beings (*thāvarā*); these eternal, pre-existing, bound, and accumulated states (*bhāva*) proclaimed by the Jinas are declared, and so forth, up to being demonstrated. Thus is it known, thus is it understood, thus is it realized; thus is the exposition of conduct (*caraṇa*) and activity (*karaṇa*) proclaimed. These, then, are the *Paṇhāvāgaraṇāiṃ*.

What then is the *Vivāgasuya* (Scripture on the Ripening of Karma)? In the *Vivāgasuya*, the ripening of the fruits of well-done and ill-done karmas is proclaimed; therein are ten accounts of the ripening of suffering and ten accounts of the ripening of happiness.

What, then, are the *duhavivāgas* (the fruits of suffering)? In the *duhavivāgas*, there are described the cities, gardens, groves, shrines, and assembly halls; the kings, parents, and spiritual teachers; the religious discourses; the specific excellences of power pertaining to this world and the next; the departures for hell; the wanderings through the cycle of existence; the successions of suffering; rebirths in low castes; and the rarity of attaining enlightenment. This, then, is the *duhavivāga*.

What, then, are the Suha-vivāgas (Accounts of Auspicious Results)? In the Suha-vivāgas, there are narrated the cities, gardens, groves, shrines, assemblies, kings, parents, spiritual teachers, religious discourses, specific worldly and otherworldly powers, renunciations of enjoyments, initiations, stages of the wandering life, mastery of sacred learning, ascetic practices, penances, fastings, renunciations of food, voluntary entry into water, rebirths in the heavens, successions of happiness, rebirths in noble families, the attainment of right faith, and final liberation. This is what constitutes the Suha-vivāgas.

Of the *Vivāgasuya*, there are limited recitations (*vāyaṇā*), numerable sub-sections (*anuogadāra*), numerable chapters (*veḍha*), numerable verses (*silōga*), numerable analytical summaries (*nijjuttī*), numerable compendia (*saṅgahaṇī*), and numerable sections (*paḍivattī*). As for its status as an *aṅga*, it is the eleventh *aṅga*, consisting of two scriptural divisions (*suyakkhandha*), twenty chapters (*ajjhayaṇa*), twenty times for formal recitation (*uddesaṇakāla*), and twenty times for detailed recitation (*samuddesaṇakāla*). It contains numerable thousands of words by word-count, numerable syllables, infinite modes of expression (*gamā*), and infinite aspects (*pajjavā*). Therein are described numerable mobile beings (*tasā*) and infinite stationary beings (*thāvarā*), as well as eternal, pre-existing, bound, and accumulated states (*bhāvā*) proclaimed by the Jinas. Thus is the self described; thus is it proclaimed. This is the *Vivāgasuya*.

What is the Diṭṭhivāya? In the Diṭṭhivāya, the exposition of all states of existence is proclaimed. It is briefly declared to be fivefold, namely: the Parikamma, the Suttas, the Puvvagaya, the Anuyoga, and the Cūliyā.

What is that "preparation" (*parikamma*)? Preparation is declared to be sevenfold, namely: the preparation of the ranks of the perfected ones (*siddhaseniyā-parikamma*), the preparation of the ranks of humans (*maṇussaseniyā-parikamma*), the preparation of the ranks of those touched [by knowledge] (*puṭṭhaseniyā-parikamma*), the preparation of the ranks of those immersed [in knowledge] (*ōgāḍhaseniyā-parikamma*), the preparation of the ranks of those who attain [knowledge] (*uvasampajaṇaseniyā-parikamma*), the preparation of the ranks of those who abandon [ignorance] (*vippajahana-seniyā-parikamma*), and the preparation of the ranks of those fallen and not fallen (*cuyācuya-seniyā-parikamma*).

What is that? The Siddhaseniyā-parikamma. The Siddhaseniyā-parikamma is taught to be of fourteen kinds, namely: the root-words (māugāpayāiṁ), synonymous words (egaṭṭhiyapayāiṁ), words with specific meanings (aṭṭhāpayāiṁ), the reading (pāḍhō), the space-words (āgāsapayāiṁ), the bridge-like (kēubhūyaṁ), the grouped (rāsibaddhaṁ), the single-fold (ēgaguṇaṁ), the double-fold (duguṇaṁ), the triple-fold (tiguṇaṁ), the bridge-like (kēubhūya), the receptacle (paḍiggahō), the cycle of existence (saṁsāra), the receptacle (paḍiggahō), the Nandāvarta (nandāvattaṁ), and the Siddhāvarta (siddhāvattaṁ). This is the Siddhaseniyā-parikamma.

What is that which constitutes the *Maṇussa-sēṇiyā-parikamma*? The *Maṇussa-sēṇiyā-parikamma* is declared to be of fourteen kinds, namely: *māugā-payāī*, *egaṭṭhiya-payāī*, *aṭṭhā-payāī*, *pāḍha*, *āgāsa-payāī*, *kēubhūya*, *rāsibaddha*, *ēgaguṇa*, *duguṇa*, *tiguṇa*, *kēubhūya-paḍiggaha*, *saṁsāra-paḍiggaha*, *naṇḍāvatta*, and *maṇussāvatta*. This is the *Maṇussa-sēṇiyā-parikamma*.

What is the *puṭṭhasēṇiyāparikamma*? The *puṭṭhasēṇiyāparikamma* is explained as being of eleven kinds, namely: *pāḍha*, *āgāsapaya*, *kēubhūya*, *rāsibaddha*, *ēgaguṇa*, *duguṇa*, *tiguṇa*, *kēubhūyapaḍiggaha*, *saṁsārapaḍiggaha*, *nandāvatta*, and *puṭṭhāvatta*. This is the *puṭṭhasēṇiyāparikamma*. What is the *ōgāḍhasēṇiyāparikamma*? It is explained as being of eleven kinds, namely: *pāḍha*, *āgāsapaya*, *kēubhūya*, *rāsibaddha*, *ēgaguṇa*, *duguṇa*, *tiguṇa*, *kēubhūyapaḍiggaha*, *saṁsārapaḍiggaha*, *nandāvatta*, and *uvasampajjaṇāvatta*. This is the *uvasampajjaṇasēṇiyāparikamma*. What is the *vippajahaṇasēṇiyāparikamma*? It is explained as being of eleven kinds, namely: *pāḍha*, *āgāsapaya*, *kēubhūya*, *rāsibaddha*, *ēgaguṇa*, *duguṇa*, *tiguṇa*, *kēubhūyapaḍiggaha*, *saṁsārapaḍiggaha*, *nandāvatta*, and *vippajahaṇāvatta*. This is the *vippajahaṇasēṇiyāparikamma*.

What is that? The *cuyācuya-śreṇī-parikarma*. It is declared to be of eleven kinds, namely: *pāṭha*, *ākāśapada*, *ketubhūta*, *rāśibaddha*, *ekaguṇa*, *dviguṇa*, *triguṇa*, *ketubhūtapratigraha*, *saṃsārapratigraha*, *nandāvarta*, and *cuyācuyāvarta*. This is the *cuyācuya-śreṇī-parikarma*. There are six *catuṣkanaiyika* [sections] and seven *tairāśika* [sections]. This concludes the *parikarmas*.

What then are the *sūtras*? Twenty-two *sūtras* are taught, namely: *ujjusuya*, *pariṇayāpariṇaya*, *bahubhaṅgiya*, *vijayacariya*, *anantara*, *parampara*, *sāmāṇa*, *sañjūha*, *sambhinna*, *āhaccāya*, *sōvatthiya*, *ghaṇṭa*, *nandāvatta*, *bahula*, *puṭṭhāpuṭṭha*, *viyāvatta*, *ēvambhūya*, *duyāvatta*, *vattamāṇuppaya*, *samabhirūḍha*, *savvaōbhadda*, *pannāsa*, *duppaḍiggaha*. These twenty-two *sūtras* follow the *chinnacchēya-naya* (the method of interrupted cutting) in the sequence of our own scriptures (*sasamayasutta*). These twenty-two *sūtras* follow the *acchinnacchēya-naya* (the method of uninterrupted cutting) in the sequence of the Ājīvika scriptures. Thus ends the section on the *Pūrvagata*. Now, what is the *Anuyoga*? The *Anuyoga* is declared to be of two kinds: namely, the *Mūlaprathamānuyoga* and the *Gaṇḍikānuyoga*. What is the *Mūlaprathamānuyoga*? In the *Mūlaprathamānuyoga*, there are recounted the previous births of the Arhats, the Blessed Ones; their ascents to the celestial realms, their lifespans, their descents, their births, their consecrations, their supreme royal splendors, their renunciations, their fierce austerities, the arising of their kevala-knowledge, their establishment of the *Tīrtha*, as well as their disciples, the *gaṇas*, the *gaṇadharas*, the female elders (*ajjās*), and the female leaders (*pravartinīs*). It also includes the numerical measure of the fourfold *saṅgha*; the Jinas, those with mind-reading knowledge (*manapajjava*), clairvoyance (*ōhināṇī*), those possessing complete scriptural knowledge (*samattasuyanāṇinō*), the eloquent speakers (*vāī*), and those who have attained the highest state (*anuttaragaī*). It describes the monks with superior transformation-bodies (*uttaravēuvviō*), how many have attained perfection (*siddhā*), the path to perfection (*siddhipahō*) as it has been taught, for how long they remained in the world, which of those supreme sages were "end-makers" (*antagaḍē*)—having destroyed a certain number of food-meals (*bhattāiṁ*) at specific places—and having escaped the flood of darkness, attained the unsurpassed bliss of liberation. These and other such matters are told in the *Mūlaprathamānuyoga*; thus ends the *Mūlaprathamānuyoga*. Now, what is the *Gaṇḍikānuyoga*? In the *Gaṇḍikānuyoga*, the *gaṇḍikās* (sections) concerning the lineage-holders (*kulagara*), the Tīrthaṅkaras, the universal monarchs (*cakravartins*), the ten heroes (*dasārakas*), the Baladevas, the Vāsudevas, the aeons of increase (*ussappiṇī*), and the intervals between thoughts (*cittantara*) are proclaimed. These and other such *gaṇḍikās* regarding the various transmigrations through the destinies of gods, humans, animals, and hell-beings are explained. Thus ends the *Gaṇḍikānuyoga*, and thus ends the *Anuyoga*.
What, then, are the *cūlikās*? The *cūlikās* are the supplements (*cūlikā*) to the first four *pūrvas*; the remaining *pūrvas* are without supplements. Such, then, are the *cūlikās*.

The *Diṭṭhivāya* has a limited number of recitations (*vāyaṇā*), a numerable number of sections (*anuogadāra*), a numerable number of chapters (*veḍha*), a numerable number of verses (*silōga*), a numerable number of sub-sections (*paḍivattī*), a numerable number of analytical expositions (*nijjuttī*), and a numerable number of summaries (*saṅgahaṇī*). In terms of its structural divisions within the *Aṅgas*, it is the twelfth *Aṅga*. It consists of one *Suyakkhandha* (scriptural section), fourteen *Puvvas* (primordial texts), a numerable number of *Vatthus* (topics), a numerable number of *Cullavatthus* (minor topics), a numerable number of *Pāhuḍas* (introductions), a numerable number of *Pāhuḍapāhuḍas* (sub-introductions), a numerable number of *Pāhuḍiyās* (introductory treatises), a numerable number of *Pāhuḍapāhuḍiyās* (sub-treatises), and a numerable number of thousands of phrases (*payasahassāiṃ*) by count of words. There are a numerable number of syllables, infinite modes (*gamā*), and infinite aspects (*pajjavā*), up to the point where they are demonstrated. Thus is the self [taught], up to the point where it is explained. This is the *Diṭṭhivāya*.

In this twelve-fold collection of the scriptures (dvādaśāṅga gaṇipiṭaka), infinite positive entities (bhāva), infinite negative entities (abhāva), infinite causes (hetu), infinite non-causes (ahetu), infinite reasons (kāraṇa), infinite non-reasons (akāraṇa), infinite souls (jīva), infinite non-souls (ajīva), infinite those destined for liberation (bhavasiddhiya), infinite those not destined for liberation (abhavasiddhiya), infinite perfected ones (siddha), and infinite non-perfected ones (asiddha) are declared.
Existence and non-existence, cause and non-cause, instrument and non-instrument, as well as soul and non-soul, the destined and the undestined, the perfected and the unperfected. (Nandī 156)

Thus, in the past, infinite beings, having violated the command of this twelve-fold collection of scriptures (*gaṇipiḍaga*), have wandered through the fourfold wilderness of *saṃsāra*. Thus, in the present time, limited beings, having violated the command of this twelve-fold collection of scriptures, are wandering through the fourfold wilderness of *saṃsāra*. Thus, in the future time, infinite beings, having violated the command of this twelve-fold collection of scriptures, will wander through the fourfold wilderness of *saṃsāra*. Thus, in the past, infinite beings, having fulfilled the command of this twelve-fold collection of scriptures, have crossed over the fourfold wilderness of *saṃsāra*. Thus, in the present time, limited beings, having fulfilled the command of this twelve-fold collection of scriptures, are crossing over the fourfold wilderness of *saṃsāra*. Thus, in the future time, infinite beings, having fulfilled the command of this twelve-fold collection of scriptures, will cross over the fourfold wilderness of *saṃsāra*. This twelve-fold collection of scriptures has never not existed, does not not exist, and will never not exist; it has existed, it exists, and it will exist. It is constant, fixed, eternal, indestructible, unchangeable, stable, and permanent. Just as, for example, the substance "opposite side" (*pañcatthikāya*) has never not existed, does not not exist, and will never not exist—it has existed, it exists, and it will exist; it is constant, fixed, eternal, indestructible, unchangeable, stable, and permanent—even so, this twelve-fold collection of scriptures has never not existed, does not not exist, and will never not exist; it has existed, it exists, and it will exist. It is constant, fixed, eternal, indestructible, unchangeable, stable, and permanent. In brief, it is declared to be fourfold: by way of substance (*davva*), by way of space (*khētta*), by way of time (*kāla*), and by way of state (*bhāva*). Therein, by way of substance, one possessing scriptural knowledge (*suyanāṇī*), when attentive, knows and sees all substances. By way of space, one possessing scriptural knowledge, when attentive, knows and sees all space. By way of time, one possessing scriptural knowledge, when attentive, knows and sees all time. By way of state, one possessing scriptural knowledge, when attentive, knows and sees all states.

The syllable (akkhara), the conscious (saṇṇī), the correct (sammaṃ), that which has a beginning (sāiyaṃ), that which indeed has an end (sapajjavasiyaṃ), the derivative (gamiyaṃ), and that which is included within the limbs (aṅgapaviṭṭhaṃ)— these seven [categories] have their opposites. (Nandī 158)

The wise ones, experts in the *pūrvas*, declare that the acquisition of scriptural knowledge (*śrutajñāna*) is seen through the eight qualities of the intellect by means of grasping the scriptures of the *āgamas*. (Nandī 159)

What is *anujñā* (permission)? *Anujñā* is declared to be sixfold, namely: name-permission (*nāmānujñā*), representation-permission (*sthāpanānujñā*), substance-permission (*dravyānujñā*), space-permission (*kṣetrānujñā*), time-permission (*kālānujñā*), and state-permission (*bhāvānujñā*). What is name-permission? Name-permission is that which is given the name "permission" (*anujñā*) for a living being (*jīva*) or a non-living thing (*ajīva*), for many living beings or many non-living things, or for both, or for many of both. That is name-permission. What is representation-permission? Representation-permission is when a representation of "permission" is established—whether in woodwork, bookwork, plasterwork, painting, or in knotted, woven, stuffed, or joined objects; whether in dice, cowrie shells, or single or multiple items; whether as a representation of reality (*sadbhāva-sthāpanā*) or a representation of unreality (*asadbhāva-sthāpanā*). That is representation-permission. What is the distinction between name and representation? A name is eternal (*āvakahika*), whereas a representation may be temporary (*ittariya*) or eternal.

What is that? It is the permission regarding substances (dravyānujñā). Permission regarding substances is declared to be twofold: namely, that which is by way of scripture (āgama) and that which is not by way of scripture (no-āgama).

What, then, is the authorization of substance (*dravyānujñā*) from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*)? Authorization of substance from the perspective of scripture is as follows: for one who has studied the word "authorization" (*anuññatti*), mastered it, fixed it, conquered it, fully mastered it—making it identical in name, identical in sound, with syllables neither deficient nor redundant, with syllables not dropped, not muddled, not confused, complete, with a complete resonance, uttered from the throat and lips, and received through the oral instruction of a teacher; yet who engages therein only in recitation, questioning, rehearsing, and religious discourse (*dhammakahā*), but not in reflection (*anuprekṣā*). Why? Because it is said, "Non-engagement is substance. According to the *Naigama* standpoint, if there is one engaged, there is one authorization of substance from the perspective of scripture; if two are engaged, there are two authorizations of substance from the perspective of scripture; if three are engaged, there are three authorizations of substance from the perspective of scripture. Thus, however many are engaged, there are that many authorizations of substance. The same applies to the *Vyavahāra* standpoint. For the *Saṅgraha* standpoint, whether one or many, whether engaged or engaged-in-general, that is one authorization of substance. For the *Rjusūtra* standpoint, if one is engaged, there is one authorization of substance from the perspective of scripture; it does not accept plurality. For the three semantic standpoints (*śabdanaya*), the cognizer (*jñātṛ*) engaged is non-substantial (*avastu*). Why? Because if he is a cognizer, he is not engaged; [if he is engaged, he is not a cognizer]. That is authorization of substance from the perspective of scripture.

What is the non-scriptural (nō-āgama) substance-permission (davvāṇunnā)? Non-scriptural substance-permission is declared to be threefold: namely, substance-permission as the body of the knower (jāṇagasarīra-davvāṇunnā), substance-permission as the body of the future being (bhaviyasarīra-davvāṇunnā), and substance-permission distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future being. What is substance-permission as the body of the knower? It is the body of one who knows the meaning of the term "permission" (aṇunna), which is free from death, decay, and abandonment, cast off by the soul, lying on a bed, on a mat, in a posture of rest (nisīhiyā), or on the surface of the Siddha-stone. [The thought: "Ah! By means of this collection of bodies, through the state seen by the Jina, the word 'permission' has been proclaimed, explained, demonstrated, shown, pointed out, and illustrated. What is the illustration? "This [body] was in a pot of ghee; this was in a pot of honey. This is substance-permission as the body of the knower. What is substance-permission as the body of the future being? It is a soul that has emerged from the birth of a womb and has assumed this very collection of bodies, [who, though not yet practicing,] will in the future learn the word "permission" through the state seen by the Jina. What is the illustration? "This will be in a pot of ghee; this will be in a pot of honey. This is substance-permission as the body of the future being. What is substance-permission distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future being? It is declared to be threefold: namely, worldly (lōiya), heterodox (kuppāvayaṇiya), and super-worldly (lōuttariya).

What is worldly permission regarding material things (*lōiyā davvāṇunnā*)? Worldly permission regarding material things is taught to be threefold: namely, with consciousness (*sacittā*), without consciousness (*acittā*), and mixed (*mīsiyā*). What is permission regarding material things with consciousness? It is as follows: for example, a king, a crown prince, a lord, a high official, a provincial governor, a householder, a wealthy merchant, a guild-leader, a general, or a caravan leader, being pleased for some reason or other, might grant permission for a horse, an elephant, a camel, an ox, a donkey, a horse, a goat, a slave, or a female slave. This is permission regarding material things with consciousness. What is permission regarding material things without consciousness? It is as follows: for example, a king, a crown prince, a lord, a high official, a provincial governor, a householder, a wealthy merchant, a general, or a caravan leader, being pleased for some reason or other, might grant permission for a seat, a bed, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a banner, a crown, silver, gold, bronze, cloth, or gems, pearls, shells, crystals, corals, red jewels, and so forth—whatever is existing, essential, and valuable. This is permission regarding material things without consciousness. What is permission regarding material things that are mixed? It is as follows: for example, a king, a crown prince, or [as before] up to a caravan leader, being pleased for some reason or other, might grant permission for an elephant adorned with ornaments on its face, or a horse adorned with a saddle and a fly-whisk, or a male slave or a female slave fully decorated with all ornaments. This is permission regarding material things that are mixed. This concludes worldly permission regarding material things.

What is that which concerns the material authorization (*davvāṇunnā*) of those belonging to false doctrines (*kuppāvayaṇiyā*)? It is declared to be threefold: namely, with living beings (*sacittā*), without living beings (*acittā*), and mixed (*mīsiyā*). What is material authorization with living beings? For example, a teacher (*āyariya*) or a preceptor (*uvajjhāya*), being pleased for some reason or another, might authorize a horse, an elephant, a camel, an ox, a donkey, a horse, a goat, a ram, a male slave, or a female slave. This is material authorization with living beings. What is material authorization without living beings? For example, a teacher or a preceptor, being pleased for some reason or another, might authorize a seat, a bed, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a headband, a crown, silver, gold, bell-metal, cloth, or gems, pearls, conch-shells, crystals, coral, red jewels, and so forth—whatever is existing, valuable, and fit to be given. This is material authorization without living beings. What is material authorization that is mixed? For example, a teacher or a preceptor, being pleased for some reason or another, might authorize an elephant adorned with ornaments on its face, a horse adorned with a saddle and a fly-whisk, or a male or female slave adorned with all kinds of ornaments. This is material authorization that is mixed. This concludes the material authorization of those belonging to false doctrines.

What is that which is the supramundane (lōuttariyā) permission of things (davvāṇunnā)? It is declared to be threefold: namely, with consciousness (sacittā), without consciousness (acittā), and mixed (mīsiyā). What is that which is the permission of things with consciousness? For example, when a teacher (āyariya), or a preceptor (uvajjhāya), or an elder (thēra), or an administrator (pavatti), or a leader of a group (gaṇī), or a holder of the scriptures (gaṇahara), or a supervisor of a group (gaṇāvacchēya), being pleased for some reason, grants permission to a disciple (sīsa) or a female disciple (sissiṇī); that is the permission of things with consciousness. What is that which is the permission of things without consciousness? For example, when a teacher, or a preceptor, or an elder, or an administrator, or a leader of a group, or a holder of the scriptures, or a supervisor of a group, being pleased for some reason, grants permission for a robe (vattha), or a bowl (pāya), or a water-strainer (paḍiggaha), or a blanket (kambala), or a broom (pāyapuñchaṇa); that is the permission of things without consciousness. What is that which is the mixed permission of things? For example, when a teacher, or a preceptor, or an elder, or an administrator, or a leader of a group, or a holder of the scriptures, or a supervisor of a group, being pleased for some reason, grants permission to a disciple or a female disciple along with their belongings and requisites (sabhaṇḍa-mattōvagaraṇa); that is the mixed permission of things. That is the supramundane permission of things. That is the permission of things distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future being. That is the permission of things from the perspective of non-scriptural knowledge (nōāgama). That is the permission of things (davvāṇunnā).

What is the authorization regarding the field (*khetta-anunnā*)? Authorization regarding the field is when one authorizes someone’s field—be it of a certain extent, or in a particular field; that is the authorization regarding the field.

What is the authorization regarding the time (*kāla-anunnā*)? Authorization regarding the time is when one authorizes someone’s time—be it for a certain duration, or at a particular time—and that is as follows: whether past, present, or future; whether in spring, winter, or the rainy season; or for the purpose of remaining stationary; that is the authorization regarding the time.

What is that which concerns the approval of dispositions (*bhāvānujñā*)? The approval of dispositions is declared to be threefold, namely: worldly (*laukika*), pertaining to false doctrines (*kupravacanīya*), and transcendent (*lokottara*).

What is the worldly sanction of dispositions (*lōiyā bhāvāṇunnā*)? Worldly sanction of dispositions is as follows: for example, when a king or a crown prince, being pleased, might grant a favor regarding some disposition of anger or the like; that is worldly sanction of dispositions. What is the sanction of dispositions of those in false doctrines (*kuppāvayaṇiyā bhāvāṇunnā*)? Sanction of dispositions of those in false doctrines is as follows: for example, when some teacher (*āyariē*) or [other preceptor] might grant a favor regarding some disposition of anger or the like; that is the sanction of dispositions of those in false doctrines. What is the supramundane sanction of dispositions (*lōuttariyā bhāvāṇunnā*)? Supramundane sanction of dispositions is as follows: for example, when a teacher or [other preceptor], being pleased for some reason, might—through a disposition pure in three ways and in the three organs—grant to a disciple who is disciplined, preeminent in forbearance and other virtues, and well-behaved, the *Āyāra*, the *Sūyagaḍa*, the *Ṭhāṇa*, the *Samavāya*, the *Vivāhapannatti*, the *Nāyādhammakaha*, the *Uvāsagadasā*, or the *Antagaḍadasā*, or the entire scriptural corpus (*savvāṇuōga*) with respect to all substances, qualities, and modifications; that is the supramundane sanction of dispositions. That is the sanction of dispositions.
What is the authorization? For whom is there authorization? For how long has the authorization for practice been in effect?
It was initiated by Purimatāla; it was for Uṣabhasena. [Nandī 2] Authorization consists of: rising up, bowing down, naming, establishing, origin, propagation, and the modes of practice.
For both of these, the essence is the path and the code of conduct. Nandī.3.

Compendium, restraint, shedding of karma, and the stabilization [of the self]—these are the means for the increase of the soul, as well as the supreme state; such are the names recognized by the wise. Nandī.4.

Knowledge is declared to be fivefold: that is, knowledge derived from direct perception (*ābhinibodhika-jñāna*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta-jñāna*), clairvoyance (*avadhi-jñāna*), telepathy (*manaḥparyaya-jñāna*), and omniscience (*kevala-jñāna*). Among these, four types of knowledge are set aside and established as such; they are not recited, not fully recited, and are not authorized for study. However, regarding scriptural knowledge, recitation, full recitation, authorization, and formal instruction do take place. If recitation, full recitation, authorization, and formal instruction take place for scriptural knowledge, does recitation, full recitation, authorization, and formal instruction take place for that which is included within the *Aṅgas*, or does recitation, full recitation, authorization, and formal instruction take place for that which is outside the *Aṅgas*? O Gautama! Recitation, full recitation, authorization, and formal instruction take place for that which is included within the *Aṅgas*, and recitation, full recitation, authorization, and formal instruction also take place for that which is outside the *Aṅgas*.

Furthermore, with reference to this formal authorization (*paṭṭhavaṇa*), the recitation (*uddesa*), detailed exposition (*samuddesa*), permission (*aṇunnā*), and instruction (*anuoga*) of the *aṅgabāhira* (texts outside the canonical divisions) proceed. Now, if the recitation, detailed exposition, permission, and instruction of the *aṅgabāhira* proceed, does the recitation, detailed exposition, permission, and instruction of the *kāliya* (texts belonging to the present time) proceed, or does the recitation, detailed exposition, permission, and instruction of the *ukkāliya* (texts belonging to other times) proceed? Gautama! The recitation, and so forth, of the *kāliya* proceeds, and the recitation, detailed exposition, permission, and instruction of the *ukkāliya* also proceeds.

Furthermore, with reference to this formal undertaking (*paṭṭhavaṇa*), the recitation (*uddesa*), the detailed recitation (*samuddesa*), the authorization (*aṇunnā*), and the instruction (*anuoga*) of the *ukkāliya* (non-essential) scriptures proceed. Just as the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and instruction of the *ukkāliya* proceed, does the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and instruction of the *āvassaga* (essential) scriptures also proceed? Or do the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and instruction of that which is distinct from the *āvassaga* proceed? [The answer is: The recitation up to the instruction of the *āvassaga* proceeds, and the recitation up to the instruction of that which is distinct from the *āvassaga* also proceeds.

If the recitation (*uddesa*), detailed recitation (*samuddesa*), authorization (*aṇunnā*), and exposition (*anuoga*) take place for the *Āvaśyaka*, do they also take place for the *Sāmāyika*, the *Caturviṃśatistava*, the *Vandana*, the *Pratikramaṇa*, the *Kāyotsarga*, and the *Pratyākhyāna*? They take place for all of these. If the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and exposition take place for what is outside the *Āvaśyaka*, do they take place for the *Kālika-śruta* (scripture of the day) or for the *Utkālika-śruta* (scripture of the night)? They take place for both the *Kālika* and the *Utkālika*.

If the recitation (*uddesa*), detailed recitation (*samuddesa*), authorization (*aṇunnā*), and exposition (*anuoga*) proceed for the *Utkālika* [scriptures], then do they also proceed for the *Daśavaikālika*, the *Kalpyākalpya*, the *Cullakappa-suya*, the *Mahākappa-suya*, the *Upapātika-suya*, the *Rājapraśnīya-suya*, the *Jīvābhigama*, the *Prajñāpanā*, the *Mahāprajñāpanā*, the *Pramādāpramāda*, the *Nandi*, the *Anuyogadvāras*, the *Devendrastava*, the *Tandulavaitālika*, the *Candravijjhaya*, the *Sūryaprajñapti* (or *Candraprajñapti*), the *Pauruṣamandala*, the *Mandalapraveśa*, the *Vidyācaraṇavinicchiya*, the *Gaṇividyā*, the *Saṃlekhanā-suya*, the *Vihārakalpa*, the *Vītarāga-suya*, the *Dhyānavibhakti*, the *Maraṇavibhakti*, the *Maraṇaviśodhi*, the *Ātavibhakti*, the *Ātaviśodhi*, the *Caraṇaviśodhi*, the *Āturapratyākhyāna*, and the *Mahāpratyākhyāna*? [The answer is: For all of these, the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and exposition proceed.

If the recitation (*uddesa*), detailed exposition (*samuddesa*), authorization (*aṇunnā*), and formal instruction (*anuoga*) proceed for the *Kāliya*, do they likewise proceed for the *Uttarajjhayaṇas*, the *Dasās*, the *Kappa*, the *Vavahāra*, the *Nisīha*, the *Mahānisīha*, the *Isibhāsiyāṇi*, the *Jambuddīvapaṇṇattī*, the *Candapaṇṇattī*, the *Dīvapaṇṇattī*, the *Sāgarapaṇṇattī*, the *Khuḍḍiyāvimāṇapavibhattī*, the *Mahalliyāvimāṇapavibhattī*, the *Aṅgacūliyā*, the *Vaggacūliyā*, the *Vivāhacūliyā*, the *Aruṇovavāya*, the *Varuṇovavāya*, the *Garulovavāya*, the *Dharaṇovavāya*, the *Vesamaṇovavāya*, the *Velandharovavāya*, the *Devindovavāya*, the *Uṭṭhāṇasuya*, the *Samuṭṭhāṇasuya*, the *Nāgapariyāvaṇiyā*, the *Nirayāvaliyā*, the *Kappiyā*, the *Kappavaḍiṁsiyā*, the *Pupphiya*, the *Pupphacūliyā*, the *Vaṇhiya*, the *Vaṇhidasā*, the *Āsīvisabhāvaṇā*, the *Diṭṭhivisabhāvaṇā*, the *Cāraṇabhāvaṇā*, the *Sumiṇabhāvaṇā*, the *Mahāsumiṇabhāvaṇā*, and the *Tēyagginisaggā*—for all these, does the recitation, detailed exposition, authorization, and formal instruction proceed?

If the recitation (*uddesa*), detailed recitation (*samuddesa*), authorization (*anujñā*), and exposition (*anuyoga*) proceed for that which is included within the *Aṅgas*, do they proceed for the *Ācārāṅga*, the *Sūtrakṛtāṅga*, the *Sthānāṅga*, the *Samavāyāṅga*, the *Vyākhyāprajñapti*, the *Jñātādharmakathā*, the *Upāsakadaśā*, the *Antakṛddaśā*, the *Anuttaraupapātikadaśā*, the *Praśnavyākaraṇa*, the *Vipākaśruta*, and the *Dṛṣṭivāda*? They proceed for all of these as well, from the recitation up to the exposition.

Furthermore, with reference to this formal initiation (*paṭṭhavaṇa*), the recitation (*uddesa*), the detailed recitation (*samuddesa*), the authorization (*aṇunnā*), and the instruction (*anuoga*) proceed for this monk and this nun. Through the hands of the venerable elders (*khamāsamaṇa*), by means of the scripture (*sutta*), the meaning (*attha*), and both together, I recite, I recite in detail, and I authorize.
